articles.title: Who Is Indigenous? The Politics of Tribal Identity Terminology in India and Bangladesh
articles.full_text:
Tribal people in South Asia prefer being called adivasi or original inhabitants, but nationalist forces in India and Bangladesh oppose it for different reasons.
Dancers and drummers of the Kurukh Oraon Adivasi community of eastern India.
On August 9, the government in the eastern Indian state of West Bengal did not host events marking the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples. Last year, the day was celebrated with events across the state over four days. The new Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government that came to power in May issued a notice on August 5, stating that this year’s celebration was cancelled. No reason was given for the decision.
West Bengal’s indigenous people’s organizations protested the move, as did the opposition parties. “This is an assault on the indigenous people’s identity and pride,” Mayukh Biswas, a leader of the West Bengal unit of the Communist Party of India-Marxists, said, alleging that the decision stemmed from the BJP’s ideological project of denying the adivasi (indigenous/aboriginal) identity of the tribal population.
Peeved by the government’s neglect, several indigenous peoples’ organizations in West Bengal took out processions to celebrate the day on August 9.
In Bangladesh on the same day, tribal groups pressed for their long-standing demand that they be called adivasi/indigenous people. As the Bangladesh government does not officially celebrate the International Day for the World’s Indigenous Peoples, tribal groups celebrated on their own.
West Bengal’s BJP government’s decision does not come as a surprise. In 2021, it formally institutionalized November 15 as “Janjatiya Gaurav Divas” (Tribal Pride Day). Since 2022, neither President Droupadi Murmu, who comes from a tribal community, nor Prime Minister Narendra Modi has shared any celebratory message on August 9. In contrast, November 15 receives extensive state patronage.
In fact, in 2024, one of the BJP’s crucial ideological partners alleged that “external forces and Christian missionaries” were seeking to divide society using Indigenous People’s Day.
The August 9 event has “indigenous people” in the name of the day. In the Indo-Aryan group of languages like Sanskrit, Hindi, Bengali, Nepali, and Sinhalese, this is best expressed by the word adivasi. The name of the November 15 event includes janajati, which translates to “tribal” in English.
The argument over what to call the tribal peoples — adivasi, janajati or upajati — may look like a dispute over vocabulary. But it is not. It is actually an argument over history, nationhood, and political rights, especially in India and Bangladesh.
The term “adivasi” literally means original inhabitants and stands closer to globally popular terms like indigenous people and aboriginal. It carries a claim of original or prior inhabitation. When linked to land, historical continuity, and collective rights, this can acquire political significance. Terms such as janajati (tribe), upajati (sub-tribe) or vanvasi (forest dwellers) do not make that claim in the same way.
This is why the term “adivasi” is also popular in Nepal and Sri Lanka. Nepali society has gone through phases of intense debate over using adivasi or janajati. However, the debate faded somewhat as Nepal legally termed them Indigenous Nationalities or Adivasi Janajati — combining adivasi and janajati, calling the two terms complementary. In Sri Lanka, the usage of adivasi is rather new, gaining popularity since the 1990s, without much of a conflict over the term.
While organizations of the tribal people prefer the term adivasi/Mulbasi/mulnibasi (indigenous/aboriginal), Hindu religious nationalists in India and different nationalist groups in Bangladesh oppose this.
In India, the Hindu nationalists, which include Modi’s BJP and its ideological-organizational parent, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), argue that “original inhabitants” would imply that other Indians are outsiders. The Sangh therefore prefers terms such as vanvasi and janajati to describe the adivasis.
In contrast, Rahul Gandhi, India’s main opposition leader, issues celebratory messages and calls adivasis the “original owners” of the land.
In Bangladesh, successive governments and sections of the political establishment have resisted recognizing the country’s tribal peoples through the term “adivasi” or Indigenous Peoples. The arguments and political positions have varied, but the stance has not changed. Officials have been formally instructed not to use adivasi in communications. The government uses upajati or Khudra Nrigoshthi (minor ethnic races). Even this year, tribal groups demanded to be called adivasi.
In contemporary international usage, Indigenous Peoples are associated with collective rights, cultural continuity, self-identification, and relationships with ancestral territories. The U.N. Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), adopted in 2007, establishes a framework for such rights, including rights relating to cultural identity, lands, and resources.
India’s Congress-led government voted for the Declaration; Bangladesh abstained, pointing to ambiguities in the Declaration, particularly the absence of an explicit definition of “indigenous people.”
The U.N. does not provide a single universal legal definition of who constitutes an Indigenous People, as it believes identifying them is more important than defining.
In Bangladesh, the arguments against calling them adivasi include: a) the Bengali-speaking people are the original inhabitants of the deltaic plains, which form the overwhelming majority of the country’s territory; b) the tribals of the hills had originally migrated from other neighboring hills that now fall in India or Myanmar; and c) granting indigenous status could create legal avenues for claims regarding autonomy, self-determination, or specialized territorial rights, which could endanger national security at the trijunction of India, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
Another intriguing argument is that as there has been a large influx of Bengali people on these lands, demands for relocating these non-tribal settlers will create further complexities and social tension. The irony is that the settler influx happened with state backing in the first place.
The Indian scenario is different. Here, the legal/constitutional term is Scheduled Tribe (ST) (anusuchit janjati). Adivasi has long been used in Indian public discourse and by official institutions alongside the constitutionally specified category of ST. People falling under the ST category enjoy certain protections, including reservations in education and jobs. There are tribal autonomous districts where non-tribals cannot purchase or own land or business.
The BJP and the wider Sangh Parivar, however, have explicitly objected to the term on ideological grounds. Since the launch of the RSS-backed Vanvasi Kalyan Ashram (VKA) in 1952, the Hindu nationalist camp has used and promoted the term vanvasi. RSS leader Ram Madhav stated that the Sangh believes that “we all are original inhabitants of this continent.”
Later, they also incorporated the term janajati and helped launch an outfit named Janjati Suraksha Manch (tribal protection committee). The VKA’s Nepal chapter calls itself Janajati Kalyan Ashram, perhaps because tribal people in Nepal live more in the hills than the forests.
Opposition parties often argue that terms like vanvasi and janajati reduce indigenous peoples to a subset of a larger Hindu civilization. In Nepal, tribal people oppose the use of janajati, arguing that jati comes from the Hindu varna (caste) system.
Therefore, in India, it is mostly the Hindu nationalist force that opposes the adivasi term. And that, too, primarily from an ideological perspective: They claim the Aryans are as much the original inhabitants of India as different tribes are — a claim scientifically unproven but essential for the Hindu nationalist pride in Vedic Aryan supremacy over world cultures.
Gandhi, however, warned that what now appears to be a war on identity can also transform into one on their traditional and historical ownership of natural resources.
On August 9, the government in the eastern Indian state of West Bengal did not host events marking the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples. Last year, the day was celebrated with events across the state over four days. The new Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government that came to power in May issued a notice on August 5, stating that this year’s celebration was cancelled. No reason was given for the decision.
West Bengal’s indigenous people’s organizations protested the move, as did the opposition parties. “This is an assault on the indigenous people’s identity and pride,” Mayukh Biswas, a leader of the West Bengal unit of the Communist Party of India-Marxists, said, alleging that the decision stemmed from the BJP’s ideological project of denying the adivasi (indigenous/aboriginal) identity of the tribal population.
Peeved by the government’s neglect, several indigenous peoples’ organizations in West Bengal took out processions to celebrate the day on August 9.
articles.summary: Tribal people in South Asia prefer being called adivasi or original inhabitants, but nationalist forces in India and Bangladesh oppose it for different reasons.

articles.title: India’s Semiconductor Journey: Old Designer, New Producer
articles.full_text:
India already has the design talent; what it needs is to turn this talent into Indian-owned companies, and to build the supplier base its fabs lack.
The fifth edition of SEMICON India closed on September 19 in New Delhi, after featuring a massive scale of over 600 exhibitors and 300 international companies across 52 countries. Themed “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem,” the exhibition-cum-conference served two objectives. For industry, it showcased expansion in India’s indigenous technology, ranging from high-performance computing and domestic processor design to system-on-chip design automation tools. On the policy front, the platform highlighted the evolution of India’s semiconductor ecosystem, stressing its expanding capabilities and role in the global semiconductor landscape.
Semicon 2.0, the second phase of the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), was approved in July 2026 with an announced outlay of around $13 billion. The mission pitches India as a trusted and reliable partner in the global semiconductor value chain. India’s Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw described the new phase as moving “from demonstrating intent to executing projects at scale.” With increasing participation from global stakeholders, India is turning its ambitions into a credible reality.
India, an old designer in the semiconductor ecosystem, is becoming a new producer. ISM 2.0’s  progress is to be measured by two key strengths: the intellectual property created by India’s talent, and the inputs its factories consume. 
India’s semiconductor journey is not a rags-to-riches developing country story. India was a capable and serious player in the industry early on. Back in the 1980s, it had a considerable semiconductor push, with only a thin gap between India and the latest semiconductor manufacturing technologies available globally. Unfortunately, India’s chip industry lost its momentum after a devastating 1989 fire at the state-run Semiconductor Complex Limited in Mohali. Then, after the 1991 economic liberalization, the zeal for at-home manufacturing diminished. Chips could be imported from abroad for less money, while Indian fabs faced thin subsidies, bureaucratic bottlenecks, and inadequate infrastructure.
Although manufacturing became a lost cause, what India tremendously excelled in was chip design. Design is the most intellectually demanding and value-dense task of the supply chain, and India hosts around 20 percent of the world’s chip design talent working out of its Global Capability Centers (GCCs). The Indian tech cities of Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Noida, and Pune harbor massive engineering talent providing R&D for firms like Intel, Qualcomm, Texas Instruments, and NXP. This part of the supply chain existed and thrived in India even  before the ISM policy and rebranding. 
No matter how impressive it sounds, domestic capabilities in designing chips for multinational companies and filing patents for foreign parent firms is one thing. Success in domestic manufacturing and design ownership is another. 
ISM 2.0 targets the ownership gap by funding full-stack Indian semiconductor IP, startups, and deployment-linked design incentives. To ensure the IP claims, the policy conditions that the strategically important chip designs supported under the scheme will be co-owned by a state agency and remain in the country. However, co-ownership of IP tends to complicate licensing, acquisitions, and the venture funding that fabless startups need to scale. How this debatable condition pans out will determine whether India’s design talent concretizes into Indian companies.
ISM 1.0 was applauded for meeting its objectives early, by approving  12 manufacturing projects, including nine packaging units, with India’s first commercial fab under construction. Despite the achievements, India still imports more than 90 percent of its chipmaking equipment. To fill this gap and develop an ecosystem, ISM 2.0 offers fiscal support to producers of semiconductor equipment, chemicals, gases, and raw materials. 
There is also a geoeconomic angle here that weighs as heavily as the domestic ownership argument. With the United States, the European Union, Japan, and South Korea all de-risking by diversifying supply chains away from geographical concentration in Taiwan and exposure to China, global players like Micron and Applied Materials are investing in India. They see India as a politically safe node in the supply chain network. Analysts have argued for strengthening chip cooperation between Japan, South Korea, and India, using complementary strengths in fabrication, market size, and labor power, to balance out the United States’ use of tariffs as geopolitical leverage. 
The risk-diversification-minded friend-shoring might benefit India as long as the China-U.S. tensions persist. While this motivation could weaken if the tension eases, that shows no signs of happening in the near future. Plus, India is not in a zero-sum game; every plant and supply facility built today strengthens its domestic base irrespective of the geoeconomic shifts of tomorrow. 
The challenge India now faces is beyond the capital-allocation problem, where the government offers subsidies and willing chipmakers strike the deal. The task is to build a domestic base of semiconductor-grade equipment and specialty chemical suppliers, which requires tacit knowledge, iterative supplier relationships, and long-term capital, complemented by sustained state support, not just a single funding cycle. This is how Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan built up their chip industries.
India already has the design talent; what it needs is to turn this talent into Indian-owned companies, and to build the supplier base its fabs lack. Amidst global de-risking and domestic ambitions, the real test of ISM 2.0 lies in India’s success in increasing Indian IP ownership and increasing the share of fabs’ inputs made in India. If both rise, India’s chip story will be the output of its full ownership endeavors, and not a byproduct of other countries’ de-risking.

articles.title: Constitutional Reform as the Lee Jae-myung Administration’s Political Watershed
articles.full_text:
South Koreans have long discussed changing the way the presidency is set up. Should it – and can it – happen now?
On September 18, President Lee Jae-myung convened a press conference. Unlike his other public appearances, this one was devoid of smiles. There were no pleasantries floated. He just trudged to the podium in his crisp dark navy suit, his presence and the ambience made heavier by the royal blue of the presidential office draped in the backdrop.
“I have been lacking fear and humility,” he said. “I shall revive the fear for the people and tackle every task more meticulously and fiercely, from a lower position of service.” 
The administration’s poor performance in opinion polls prompted this sense of crisis and humble words. Lee’s approval ratings have been taking a steady dive since the June local elections. 
Until late August, the two main factors behind the slide had been the government’s controversial housing policy and the Democratic Party’s much more controversial judicial reform, which entrusts all investigative powers to the police. That change seems premature, or even inappropriate, given the recent barrage of anecdotes of police corruption and incompetence. 
In September, Lee’s approval ratings plummeted still more following his ill-fated Cabinet nominations. Back in 2021, Kim Seung-won, Lee’s pick for the justice minister, allegedly streamlined the drug approval process for a pharmaceutical company on behalf of his friend. This allegation resurfaced during nomination hearings. 
Meanwhile, Lee picked Yong Hye-in, the only parliamentarian from the Basic Income Party, to lead the gender equality ministry. Yong’s insistence on holding both positions, however, garnered opprobrium. 
As opposed to constituency legislators – those who won the most votes from their districts – proportional representatives like Yong owe their positions to their parties. South Korea’s proportional representation ballot, designed to give minor parties a chance at lawmaking, accounts for 46 out of the National Assembly’s 300 total seats. Legislators in these seats are expected to resign when they take up another government job since someone else from their party can replace them without tarnishing the voters’ mandate. It seemed apparent that Yong had no other reason to retain her legislative seat than to enjoy the perks of being a lawmaker.
Kim and Yong both withdrew from their ministerial nominations after much damage to the Lee administration. And now they are both under investigation, the former for alleged sexual harassment of his former staff and the latter for allegedly funneling her political funds to her husband.
The public smarts all the more to questionable behavior by liberal figures. Lee’s approval ratings in major polls hit a nadir in mid-September, dropping to 33.8 percent in a poll by Realmeter and 37 percent in another by Gallup. 
So, Lee’s press conference was a revolving door of apology and resolution to do better on all the factors shaving his approval ratings. But the most emphatic point he made – and the one that received the most headlines – was his assertion that “I have no intention whatsoever for a second presidential term.” 
The current South Korean constitution allows the president to serve a single five-year term. In 2025, when Lee was running for the snap presidential election following Yoon Suk-yeol’s impeachment, one of his campaign policies was to amend the constitution so that the president can serve two four-year consecutive terms. At the time, almost two thirds of the voters approved of such reform. 
South Korea’s system of a single five-year term for the president has come under much flak. The populace has to wait too long until they can pass judgment on the president through ballots. Besides, without the prospect of another term, the incumbent president has no incentive to behave responsibly when it comes to their government. How frequently the people can make their voices heard through voting and how much accountability with which the president leads the country determine the soundness of democracy. And South Korea has been poor in this aspect.
On top of that, the strong, centralized nature of South Korea’s presidency – often called an “imperial presidency” – has exacerbated the problem. Consider the president’s monopoly on administrative decisions; the government’s monopoly on funding for the rest of the country; the president’s power to appoint some 10,000 top government agency and QUANGO posts; the president’s authority to wield some $400 billion through their budgetary decisions; their decrees overriding local government ordinances; and the National Assembly’s inability to monitor and check the president’s executive arms. 
Yoon’s presidency manifested everything that could go wrong, from rampant corruption due to lack of auditory mechanisms to toxic control over law enforcement. South Korea’s presidency depends too much on the good will of that one person at the top. 
Naturally, constitutional reform to trim down the imperial presidency and beef up the parliament and local government has been expected to materialize sometime soon. But the speaker of the National Assembly sparked an intense controversy in late July when he said that “the question of allowing the incumbent president to serve consecutively is ultimately up to the public.” The opposition People Power Party (PPP) immediately raised the possibility that Lee could be plotting “treason” by assuming another term. 
In fact, the current constitution bars any constitutional reform – whether that’s to prolong the presidential tenure or introduce multiple terms – from applying to the incumbent president. Immediately after, the speaker admitted his error in legal interpretation. 
The presidential office also clarified to the press that, when it comes to Lee running for re-election, “our constitution doesn’t allow it, the people won’t condone it, and it’s realistically impossible.” Lee, while visiting France on September 10, mentioned again that “the constitution clearly confines my term.” 
Still, the controversy had gained enough traction to drag down his approval ratings ever since. Hence Lee’s forceful, articulate reminder during the September 18 press conference that the notion of him serving consecutive terms “is not only constitutionally impossible but also never have I thought of it.”
Lee then proposed to collaborate with the National Assembly to amend the constitution to allow for consecutive presidential terms – for future presidents, not for himself – and more even distribution of powers among the parliament and the central and local governments. He also didn’t fail to point out that this would require “bipartisan discussion and public opinion and ideas.”
Despite Lee’s fairly categorical stance, the PPP is deliberately incredulous. “Lee says he has ‘no intention’ of serving another term. Why is it so hard for him to say ‘I will not serve another term?’” wrote Jang Dong-hyuk, the PPP leader, on his social media. To him, Lee didn’t promise anything, therefore “he hasn’t given up the dream of a second consecutive term.”
The PPP floor leader, Jeong Jeom-sig, also made it clear that the PPP wouldn’t partake in any discussion for constitutional reform during the Lee administration. “The PPP is telling you now: There will be no constitutional reform during this administration,” he said to much applause among fellow PPP legislators. Like Jang, Jeong suspects that Lee has an ulterior motive to amend the constitution and run for a second term. (The president is immune from indictment, which is why the trials in various legal cases against Lee are currently on hold.)
But the real reason behind the PPP’s refusal to hash out a constitutional reform could be that it can’t take the lead in remolding the constitution to its taste. Constitutional amendment requires 200 votes in favor. The PPP only commands 109 out of 300 parliamentary seats. Meanwhile, the liberal camp comprises more than 180 seats, with the DP holding the parliamentary majority alone with its 161 seats. The PPP would manage to eke out only a piecemeal compromise at the negotiating table.
Besides, history would only remember the Lee administration, not the PPP, for having reformed the constitution. The PPP is loathe to serve Lee and the DP such an enormous political cachet on a silver platter.
In spite of the PPP’s intransigence, the DP is plowing ahead. On September 20, the DP launched a constitutional amendment committee. “It’s time to stop picking at diction but start discussing constitutional reform,” said Kim Min-seok, the DP’s new leader. 
Granted, the timing is convenient for the Lee administration. Public discourse and political haggling over constitutional amendment could overshadow any other agenda. In the process, the government’s sore spots could be covered and even forgotten. 
Plus, constitutional reform is not a distant possibility. Although the PPP opposes talk for tweaking the constitution, the conservative bloc is fractious anyways. Quite a sizable pocket despises Jang and the PPP leadership. Breakaway participation and votes are possible for constitutional amendment. Hearsay has it that some in the PPP are already stirring to join the discussion for constitutional amendment. 
Notably, Kim Tae-ho, a four-term PPP legislator, sounded the bugle of reason this time after Lee’s press conference. “We should end this war of attrition over this consecutive terms controversy,” he said on his social media, alluding to the PPP’s pathological distrust of Lee. He then underlined the need to reform the constitution “in order to disperse the authority channeled into the president and overcome the political polarization.”
But in the end, it is this “political polarization” that will be hindering the very first step needed to heal this polarization. According to Realmeter’s September 22 survey, 5 out of 10 South Koreans were still dubious about Lee’s true intentions for wanting to introduce a consecutive presidential tenure. No matter how well-meaning and earnest the government may be about reforming the constitution and the polity, if the public isn’t convinced and comforted, no talk of constitutional reform, nor any resulting constitution, would be viable. 
On September 18, President Lee Jae-myung convened a press conference. Unlike his other public appearances, this one was devoid of smiles. There were no pleasantries floated. He just trudged to the podium in his crisp dark navy suit, his presence and the ambience made heavier by the royal blue of the presidential office draped in the backdrop.
articles.summary: South Koreans have long discussed changing the way the presidency is set up. Should it – and can it – happen now?

articles.title: Takaichi’s Pre-emptive Diplomacy: What Japan Needs From the Trump-Xi Summit
articles.full_text:
Prime Minister Takaichi made Tokyo’s concerns clear to Trump before Xi Jinping arrived in Washington. Will that actually impact the summit?
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae meets with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, Sep. 22, 2026.
When Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae sat down with U.S. President Donald Trump in New York on September 22, the timing itself was the message. Chinese President Xi Jinping would arrive in Washington, D.C. the next day for state visit to Washington and his second summit with Trump this year. Takaichi said afterward that holding the talks at such a moment demonstrated the strength of the Japan-U.S. alliance. But the most important audience may have been Trump himself.
Tokyo’s anxiety is not hard to understand. Trump personally greeted Xi on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, an unusually warm welcome for a visiting foreign leader. Xi, for his part, struck a conciliatory tone upon arrival, declaring in a written statement that China and the United States “should be partners, not rivals.”
The hospitality will continue at the White House, with an elaborate welcoming ceremony and a state dinner. But expectations for substantive breakthroughs remain low. Washington and Beijing still face deep divisions over trade, artificial intelligence, Taiwan, and other issues.
With U.S. midterm elections about six weeks away, Trump has strong incentives to secure tangible economic results from China. Just before the summit, Washington and Beijing agreed to extend their trade truce by another two months, until January 10, postponing additional tariffs and export restrictions. The agreement reduces the immediate risk of renewed confrontation while giving both sides more time to negotiate.
For Tokyo, however, one concern stands above the economic bargaining: Taiwan.
China strongly opposes U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, while Trump has described such sales as a bargaining chip. Xi could use Trump’s desire for a broader economic deal to press Washington to continue delaying arms sales to the island. That has fueled concern in Tokyo that Taiwan could become part of a wider bargain between Washington and Beijing.
For Japan, Taiwan is a critical security issue. Japan’s southwestern islands lie close to Taiwan, and Takaichi’s remarks in the Diet last November that a Chinese use of force against Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan triggered a sustained Chinese pressure campaign against Tokyo. Any significant weakening of U.S. support for Taiwan could therefore have direct implications for Japan’s security and for deterrence across the Western Pacific.
That made Takaichi’s meeting with Trump more than a routine alliance check-in. According to the Japanese government, the two leaders discussed the economy, issues related to China (including economic security, AI , semiconductors, and critical minerals), and North Korea, and exchanged views on China with the Trump-Xi summit specifically in mind. Takaichi also said Japan hoped stable China-U.S. relations would contribute to international stability. 
Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu, who attended the Takaichi-Trump meeting, told NHK ahead of the Trump-Xi summit that he believed Washington’s position on Taiwan remained unchanged from the leaders’ previous summit in May. Motegi said he believed Japan and the United States shared an understanding on this point.
Whether or not that is the case will become clearer only after Trump’s talks with Xi – particularly in how Washington handles Taiwan.
Takaichi’s U.N. General Assembly speech on the same day as her meeting with Trump illustrated the other side of her China diplomacy. She declared that the “stable post-Cold War era” was over and warned that the international order based on the rule of law was facing serious challenges. She explicitly named Russia over its invasion of Ukraine and North Korea over its nuclear and missile programs. Yet she did not mention China by name, saying instead that unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion must not be tolerated anywhere in the world.
The omission was notable after months of deteriorating China-Japan relations. It suggests that while Takaichi wants Washington to remain firm in the face of Chinese pressure, Tokyo is also seeking to prevent a further deterioration in its own relationship with Beijing.
That approach fits the broader diplomatic environment surrounding the Trump-Xi meeting. Despite fierce competition over trade, technology, and AI, both Washington and Beijing appear interested, at least for now, in managing their rivalry rather than allowing it to spiral into another confrontation. Xi’s message that the two countries should be “partners, not rivals,” and the extension of the trade truce both point in that direction.
For Japan, stable China-U.S. relations are desirable. But stability achieved through a bargain that changes Washington’s approach to Taiwan would present a very different calculation for Tokyo.
Takaichi made Japan’s concerns clear before Xi arrived in Washington. The Trump-Xi summit will show whether those concerns figure in Trump’s calculations – and whether his pursuit of deals with Beijing changes the strategic environment Japan must navigate.

Despite fierce competition over trade, technology, and AI, both Washington and Beijing appear interested, at least for now, in managing their rivalry rather than allowing it to spiral into another confrontation. Xi’s message that the two countries should be “partners, not rivals,” and the extension of the trade truce both point in that direction.
articles.summary: Prime Minister Takaichi made Tokyo’s concerns clear to Trump before Xi Jinping arrived in Washington. Will that actually impact the summit?

articles.title: Grand Strategic Compatibility: The Basis of The Japan-Vietnam Partnership
articles.full_text:
The quick pace of reconciliation between Tokyo and Hanoi since the end of the Cold War has reflected the compatibility of their respective grand strategies.
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae meets with Vietnam’s President and Communist Party chief To Lam, in Hanoi, Vietnam, May. 2, 2026.
In an address to Vietnam National University in Hanoi in May, Japan’s Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae affirmed Japan’s commitment to the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) concept. Tokyo pledged to increase its political, economic, and defense cooperation with ASEAN so that each ASEAN state can “acquire autonomy and resilience” in the face of intensifying geopolitical competition. It was Takaichi’s first public address on updating her predecessor Abe Shinzo’s FOIP vision, and her decision to deliver it in Vietnam says a lot about the current state of Japan-Vietnam ties.
The reconciliation between Japan and Vietnam since the end of the Cold War has been nothing short of extraordinary. During the Third Indochina War (1978-1991), Japan sided with China and the United States to isolate Vietnam due to its status as a Soviet ally. Japan’s alignment was rooted in its fear of a Soviet invasion from the north in the late 1970s. Beginning in May 1978, Moscow had increased the number of troops stationed on Soviet-controlled Southern Kuril Islands up to 6,000. The Soviets also built up their Pacific Fleet until it became the largest of the four Soviet fleets, and they deployed the SS-20 intermediate-range ballistic missiles to the Asia-Pacific theater.
Consequently, Japan signed a Treaty of Peace and Friendship with China in August, which included an anti-hegemony clause implicitly directed against the Soviet Union. Japan strengthened naval cooperation with the United States and participated in the Rim of the Pacific Exercise for the first time ever in 1980. It also built up its own navy and air force to balance against the Soviet threat and hedge against the possibility of the U.S. retrenchment from the Asia-Pacific. The goal was to protect not only the home islands but also the sea lines of communication up to 1,000 nautical miles from Japan’s coasts.
Japan had provided economic aid to Vietnam between 1975 and 1976 to help it recover from the Second Indochina War, but after Hanoi formally allied with Moscow in November 1978 and invaded Cambodia to topple the Khmer Rouge in December, Tokyo quickly froze aid. It then failed to condemn China’s retaliatory invasion of Vietnam a few months later. In April 1979, Japan conditioned the resumption of economic aid to Vietnam on Hanoi not establishing permanent Soviet military bases in Danang and Cam Ranh Bay, which Japan worried would threaten the supply of oil from the Middle East. As Vietnam proceeded to host Soviet armed forces and occupied Cambodia during the 1980s, Japan added another condition to aid resumption, which was Vietnam’s troop withdrawal from Cambodia. Japan didn’t resume aid until 1992, after the Soviet collapse and the signing of the Paris Peace Agreements on Cambodia.
Since then, Japan’s Official Development Assistance to Vietnam has totaled approximately $29.3 billion, the largest of any Vietnam’s foreign donors. Japan is Vietnam’s third largest investor and fourth largest trading partner. Both countries began low-level defense exchanges around the same time with agreements reached over Japanese ships’ port calls in Vietnam, joint search-and-rescue operations in the South China Sea, and training of Vietnamese students at Japan’s National Defense Academy. In 2014, Japan agreed to provide Vietnam with six used vessels and six years later with technologies for building military ships to boost Hanoi’s maritime capability. In 2021, Japan signed an agreement with Vietnam to allow for the transfer of defense equipment and technology.
Vietnam falls under the scope of Japan’s new Official Security Assistance under the 2022 National Security Strategy. In 2026, Tokyo lifted a ban on the export of lethal weapons, which would allow it to sell fighter jets, missiles, and warships. Unlike with other Asian countries, the issue of Japan’s crimes committed during World War II do not cloud bilateral relations with Vietnam. The country is now one of the most pro-Japan countries in Asia. Vietnam established a partnership with Japan in 2002 and later a strategic partnership in 2009. Vietnam elevated Japan to the status of a Comprehensive Strategic Partner in 2023.
The quick pace of Japan-Vietnam reconciliation has to do with the compatibility of their respective grand strategies. During the Third Indochina War, Vietnam prioritized western and northern Indochina over the South China Sea, while Japan was occupied with defending against a Soviet invasion from the Southern Kurils. There was little cooperation during this period. After the Third Indochina War, Hanoi and Tokyo shared the same concerns over China’s contestation of their respective maritime sovereignties. Vietnam began to look east to the sea while Japan slowly pivoted to the southern islands and considered maritime zones outside of Northeast Asia vital to its security. In this context, Japan supports the combination of the East China Sea and the South China Sea into a single theater of operation.
Political leaders from both countries began to develop grand strategic visions that are compatible in terms of economy, military, and diplomacy. Vietnam’s post-1991 turn to the sea entails the development of a maritime economy, the modernization of its navy and air force, and the peaceful settlement of the South China Sea disputes via international arbitration. Likewise, Japan’s FOIP, first laid out in 2007, emphasized the securing of sea lanes stretching from the Indian Ocean to the Pacific Ocean for economic exchanges. Its 2010 National Defense Program Guidelines called for a new “dynamic defense force” away from Cold War-era style equipment and organizations capable of responding to threat from the southwest, and its 2013 National Security Strategy opposed any unilateral attempts to change the status quo in the East and South China seas in violation of international law.
Japan-Vietnam joint statements show an evolution of compatibility in their respective grand strategies. Before China submitted its “nine-dash line” map to the United Nations in 2009, Japanese and Vietnamese leaders did not emphasize maritime security in their joint statements, although there were low-level defense exchanges. Statements released by both sides in 2007 and the 2008 did not mention maritime cooperation at all, and economic cooperation was the main topic of discussion. After Beijing’s move, however, maritime cooperation became one of the key tenets of bilateral ties. Tokyo and Hanoi incrementally discussed maritime cooperation as a measure to safeguard regional peace in joint statements issued in 2010 and 2011. The 2014 joint statement mentioned maritime security as an area of cooperation for the Vietnam-Japan partnership, the same year Japan provided Vietnam six vessels and one year after Japan protested China’s declaration of an Air Defense Identification Zone over the East China Sea. The 2015, 2018, 2023, and 2025 joint statements likewise underlined the importance of maritime security.
A joint grand strategic focus on maritime security has also guided Japan’s provision of economic aid and military equipment to Vietnam. Japan wants to boost Vietnam’s economic resilience in case of Chinese economic retaliations against Vietnam’s assertion of its maritime claims. Japan’s ODA has helped Vietnam strengthen its manufacturing capability and lessen Vietnam’s need for Chinese investment under Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative. It has also pledged to deepen cooperation over energy, critical minerals, semiconductors, supply chains, and artificial intelligence. Japan’s transfer of naval technology, platforms, and expertise to Vietnam serve to secure the South China Sea sea lanes and the flow of oil from the Middle East to Japan.
The recent proposal to jointly develop fast landing crafts indicates Japan’s support for Vietnam holding and possibly retaking offshore islands. Defense cooperation is poised to go upward as Japan expands its OSA budget. In terms of diplomacy, Japan’s frequent calls to Vietnam’s ports help build a consensus and expectations for future U.S. port calls. Major U.S. Navy visits to Vietnam’s ports are often preceded by Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF) visits. Closer Japan-Vietnam diplomatic ties also allow Japan to augment its relations with ASEAN. Japan’s opposition to unilateral changes in the South China Sea supports its case for condemning China’s assertiveness in the East China Sea.
Although Japan is not a great power and cannot defend Vietnam due to legal and material constraints, Vietnam welcomes close maritime cooperation with Japan, which helps to strengthen Vietnam’s multilateral foreign policy. Japan’s constitutional constraints on fighting overseas wars have meant that Vietnam can evade the stigma of siding with one country against another, which is a principle of Hanoi’s Four Nos doctrine. Moreover, Tokyo’s economic and military assistance do not carry any conditions on human rights or pose a threat to the political authority of the Communist Party of Vietnam to the degree of those from the West. Importantly, a close relationship with Japan prevents Tokyo from seeing Hanoi’s island reclamation activities as a threat to its sea lines of communication the way it sees Beijing’s activities. Vietnam supports Japan becoming a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, a position that China opposes.
So long as Japan’s and Vietnam’s grand strategies align over the South China Sea, bilateral ties will continue to improve. There are still grounds for an expansion of cooperation. Currently, the Vietnam People’s Navy and the JMSDF spearhead defense cooperation. Their land forces have not played much role. articles.title: In India, Death Sentences Are Mostly the Result of Arbitrary Exercise of Judicial Power
articles.full_text:
Recently, a district judge awarded 23 death sentences in ten cases over a span of four months.
Earlier this month, a judge in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh hit the headlines for delivering 23 death sentences in just four months. Judge Ravi Kumar Diwakar’s 23rd death sentence involved a dowry death case where the man had burnt his wife over dowry demands. In his order, the judge made a grandiose claim that he would “prefer death than to be called a coward judge.” He alleged he was being targeted by “mafias, gangsters, criminals.”
Incidentally, Uttar Pradesh stands first in the country with regard to the number of death sentences being handed out.
Under Indian jurisprudence, only the “rarest of rare cases” justify the sentencing of a convict to death. However, Diwakar dispensed the death penalty rather freely, awarding 23 death sentences in just 10 cases. Alarmed by his propensity to award capital punishment, the more senior District Judge Virendra Kumar Singh transferred nearly 100 cases dealing with heinous crimes to his own court in August.
Diwakar’s verdicts drew public attention to the larger issue of capital punishment in India. While permitted only in the “rarest of rare” instances, the death penalty, in practice, is being awarded on the discretionary views of the judge.
Capital punishment is controversial and has triggered heated discussion in the past as well. While it is often welcomed by the public, especially in cases of brutal rape and murder, critics argue that the death penalty should not be allowed in a civilized society.
Under Indian law, when the death penalty is handed out by a lower court, it needs to be ratified or adjudicated by the higher court, including the Supreme Court. If the courts uphold the death sentence, the president of India has the power to decide on a mercy petition or clemency plea of the convict. The president can commute the death sentence to rigorous imprisonment, grant remission, or even pardon the convict.
Pranab Mukherjee, who was India’s president between 2012-2017, earned a reputation for being unsympathetic to mercy or clemency pleas. During his tenure, 34 mercy pleas came before him; he rejected 30 of them and commuted four to life imprisonment. Three executions were carried out while he was in office – that of 1993 Mumbai blast accused Yakub Memon, Parliament attack accused Afzal Guru and 26/11 Mumbai terrorist attack accused Ajmal Kasab.
Mukherjee was unlike any of his predecessors. President Pratibha Patil was the most lenient; she commuted 34 death sentences and rejected five mercy petitions. While President K.R. Narayanan, an erudite man, did not decide on any mercy plea, President Abdul Kalam, a missile scientist, decided on only two, commuting the death sentence in one case and rejecting the other. They chose to leave to their successors the difficult decision of sending a man to the gallows.
Statistics reveal a troubling reality. Indian trial courts have been meting out death sentences rather easily. In the majority of these cases, the punishment falls through when examined by higher courts.
According to the legal news portal, Law Beat, “364 wrongful convictions have been recorded in capital cases over the past decade.” Since 2023, the Supreme Court has not confirmed any death sentence, citing procedural errors and wrongful convictions by lower courts.
According to the Death Penalty in India Report 2000- 2015, of the 1,486 prisoners sentenced to death by trial courts, only 73 death sentences (5 percent) of the total were confirmed by higher courts. So, a whopping 95 percent of death sentences were thrown out by the higher courts.
Particularly shocking is the fact that over a quarter of those sentenced to death were actually innocent. Of the 1,486 individuals sentenced to death, as many as 443, i.e., 29 percent, were found by higher courts to be “not just undeserving of the death sentence but actually to be innocent of the crime for which they were being sent to the gallows.”
India’s criminal justice system is notorious for its slow delivery of justice. Those convicted spend years in jail, several on death row, before their appeals are finally decided, commuted, or acquitted. As of December 2025, approximately 574 individuals remained on death row, the highest figure this century.
Proponents of the death penalty have often argued that it deters people from committing brutal crimes. However, global human rights watchdogs like Amnesty International have reiterated that there is no evidence that capital punishment deters crime, including crimes against women like sexual assault.
Yet the clamor for the death penalty increases when heinous crimes, which evoke public outrage, occur. This was the case, for example, when “Nirbhaya,” a young woman, was brutally gang-raped in a moving bus in New Delhi in December 2012. She was thrown out on the streets with her entrails hanging out. When she subsequently died, the clamor for the accused to be hanged increased.
When sexual violence laws were reformed in 2013, the death penalty was included among the penalties for sexual assault. In cases of rape leading to the victim’s death or resulting in her being left in a “persistent vegetative state,” and rape by repeat offenders, the maximum sentence could be death. The rape laws also expanded the definition of rape and criminalized acts including stalking, voyeurism, and acid attacks.
These stringent punishments have not deterred rape. It is not the severity of punishment that deters crime but the certainty of conviction and punishment that could deter it.
Rights activists have argued that rather than knee-jerk reactions like awarding the death penalty, what is required is systemic reform of the criminal justice system, police reforms, better investigations, and access to justice. An analysis of the profile of convicts reveals that capital punishment impacts the poor and marginalized members of society more severely due to a lack of proper legal representation.
In 2019, Justice Kurian Joseph, while commuting a death sentence to life imprisonment, urged that the death penalty in India be reviewed. He noted that trial courts had been awarding it “arbitrarily and freakishly” under the influence of “emotionally charged public and media discourse.”
Under the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita (formerly the Indian Penal Code), awarding the death penalty is the absolute exception, in the “rarest of rare” cases. Before awarding it, the court needs to ascertain why the alternative option of life imprisonment cannot be handed out instead. Also, as per the law, the judge must actively consider mitigating circumstances (such as the criminal’s age, mental health, and potential for rehabilitation/ reform) along with the aggravating severity of the crime.
Although there is no evidence that capital punishment deters crime, the Indian political class and society at large continue to demand and justify the death penalty.
Globally, countries are working toward abolishing capital punishment, but India refuses to abolish it. It is ironic that India prides itself on having a human rights-based criminal justice system where even the accused are not denied fundamental rights. Yet its judicial system continues to mete out an outdated and “inhumane punishment” of the death penalty.

articles.title: Cambodian Beauty Pageant Acknowledges Mistaken Use of Thai Historical Photograph
articles.full_text:
The unresolved border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand has given rise to a rash of online disputes over cultural “ownership.”
A photograph of Thai women taken in Kamphaeng Phet province in 1906, during the reign of King Chulalongkorn.
The organizers of a Cambodian beauty pageant have been forced to acknowledge their use of a historical photograph from Thailand, saying the mistake was unintentional and resulted from “insufficient verification” of the original sources.
The Miss Universe Cambodia pageant came under fire on social media after images of women dressed in traditional attire were displayed on stage during the pageant’s preliminary round last week, along with a description saying they were wearing traditional Khmer clothing.
One of the photographs, which showed seven Thai women in traditional dress, was taken in Kamphaeng Phet province in 1906, during the reign of King Chulalongkorn. According to the Bangkok Post, the photograph is part of a large collection of glass-plate negatives that is preserved at the Phra Vajirayana Royal Library in Bangkok.
The revelation prompted a social media flame-war between Thai and Cambodian nationalists, each of whom accused the other of stealing or appropriating the other’s culture.
Thailand’s Ministry of Culture subsequently sent a letter to the pageant organizers on Monday, demanding an apology and correction for its use of the Thai photograph, which it said “was done intentionally to cause misunderstanding about the picture’s origin,” the Bangkok Post reported. Culture Minister Sabeeda Thaised told reporters that the original photograph contained a watermark, which the Miss Universe Cambodia organizers appeared to have cropped out.
The Miss Universe Cambodia statement, signed by the pageant’s national director Prasat Davin, said that the photograph was intended to highlight the traditional sbai garment, and that its incorrect attribution resulted from “insufficient verification of the original sources of those images.”
“We would like to emphasize that there was no intention to cause misunderstanding, controversy or offend the feelings of any member of the public, whether nationally or internationally,” it said.
Disputes over cultural “ownership” have been a perennial occurrence in relations between Thailand and Cambodia. A long history of cultural cross-pollination between the two nations and their respective premodern civilizations has produced a close overlap in cultural practices, including dance, cuisine, architecture, and sports like kick-boxing, as well as the two countries’ Sanskrit-derived writing systems. In spite of these cultural affinities, or perhaps because of them, the question of ownership is a highly emotive issue – one that can sometimes have real-world impacts.
For instance, in 2003, Khmer-language press reports claimed that a Thai actress said that Cambodia had “stolen” Angkor Wat, and that she would not visit the country until it was “returned” to Thailand. In response, mobs of protesters sacked the Thai Embassy and numerous Thai businesses, causing millions of dollars in damage.
Such cultural disputes have also complicated the resolution of the long-standing frontier dispute between Cambodia and Thailand. The two nations’ land border is dotted with ancient Khmer temples that are shot through with nationalist significance, particularly for the Cambodian side. One of these is Preah Vihear temple, a glorious 11th-century Angkorian temple perched on a cliff on the two nations’ border.
In 1962, the International Court of Justice ruled that Preah Vihear belonged to Cambodia, but Thai nationalists have never accepted the verdict. When UNESCO listed the temple as a World Heritage Site in 2008, royalist protesters heaped pressure on the Thai government and helped precipitate a bilateral crisis that flared into armed conflict on several occasions between 2008 and 2011.
The border dispute again resulted in armed conflict on two occasions last year, embittering relations between Phnom Penh and Bangkok – and between dueling nationalist cohorts online. In the context of the current stand-off, Thai-Cambodian disputes over cultural ownership have become more acute and potentially combustive than ever.

One of the photographs, which showed seven Thai women in traditional dress, was taken in Kamphaeng Phet province in 1906, during the reign of King Chulalongkorn. According to the Bangkok Post, the photograph is part of a large collection of glass-plate negatives that is preserved at the Phra Vajirayana Royal Library in Bangkok.
The revelation prompted a social media flame-war between Thai and Cambodian nationalists, each of whom accused the other of stealing or appropriating the other’s culture.
Thailand’s Ministry of Culture subsequently sent a letter to the pageant organizers on Monday, demanding an apology and correction for its use of the Thai photograph, which it said “was done intentionally to cause misunderstanding about the picture’s origin,” the Bangkok Post reported. Culture Minister Sabeeda Thaised told reporters that the original photograph contained a watermark, which the Miss Universe Cambodia organizers appeared to have cropped out.
The Miss Universe Cambodia statement, signed by the pageant’s national director Prasat Davin, said that the photograph was intended to highlight the traditional sbai garment, and that its incorrect attribution resulted from “insufficient verification of the original sources of those images.”
“We would like to emphasize that there was no intention to cause misunderstanding, controversy or offend the feelings of any member of the public, whether nationally or internationally,” it said.
Disputes over cultural “ownership” have been a perennial occurrence in relations between Thailand and Cambodia. A long history of cultural cross-pollination between the two nations and their respective premodern civilizations has produced a close overlap in cultural practices, including dance, cuisine, architecture, and sports like kick-boxing, as well as the two countries’ Sanskrit-derived writing systems. In spite of these cultural affinities, or perhaps because of them, the question of ownership is a highly emotive issue – one that can sometimes have real-world impacts.
For instance, in 2003, Khmer-language press reports claimed that a Thai actress said that Cambodia had “stolen” Angkor Wat, and that she would not visit the country until it was “returned” to Thailand. In response, mobs of protesters sacked the Thai Embassy and numerous Thai businesses, causing millions of dollars in damage.
Such cultural disputes have also complicated the resolution of the long-standing frontier dispute between Cambodia and Thailand. The two nations’ land border is dotted with ancient Khmer temples that are shot through with nationalist significance, particularly for the Cambodian side. One of these is Preah Vihear temple, a glorious 11th-century Angkorian temple perched on a cliff on the two nations’ border.
In 1962, the International Court of Justice ruled that Preah Vihear belonged to Cambodia, but Thai nationalists have never accepted the verdict. When UNESCO listed the temple as a World Heritage Site in 2008, royalist protesters heaped pressure on the Thai government and helped precipitate a bilateral crisis that flared into armed conflict on several occasions between 2008 and 2011.
The border dispute again resulted in armed conflict on two occasions last year, embittering relations between Phnom Penh and Bangkok – and between dueling nationalist cohorts online. In the context of the current stand-off, Thai-Cambodian disputes over cultural ownership have become more acute and potentially combustive than ever.
The organizers of a Cambodian beauty pageant have been forced to acknowledge their use of a historical photograph from Thailand, saying the mistake was unintentional and resulted from “insufficient verification” of the original sources.
The Miss Universe Cambodia pageant came under fire on social media after images of women dressed in traditional attire were displayed on stage during the pageant’s preliminary round last week, along with a description saying they were wearing traditional Khmer clothing.
Sebastian Strangio is Southeast Asia editor at The Diplomat.
articles.summary: The unresolved border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand has given rise to a rash of online disputes over cultural "ownership."

articles.title: Delivered to the Wrong Address? F-35 Parts Re-routed to Hong Kong
articles.full_text:
The F-35 is a supremely advanced fighter aircraft with many proprietary components that would be of immense value to several foreign intelligence services. It is also a consumer product.
A U.S. Air Force F-35A Lightning II, assigned to the 158th Fighter Wing, takes off from Burlington International Airport in South Burlington, Vermont, March 11, 2026.
Last summer a shipment of F-35 parts was reportedly re-routed to Hong Kong from its intended destination in Australia. Australia is a partner in the F-35 program; the People’s Republic of China is not. U.S. authorities are reportedly trying to recover the parts and prevent future breaches. The incident has caused consternation in the United States and Australia, both of which have effectively committed to the F-35 as the foundation of their future airpower. And yet the mis-shipment has made clear a fundamental contradiction at the heart of the F-35 project; high tech proprietary classification does not go well with an aggressive policy of export and offshoring. 
In short, it’s hard to keep aspects of the F-35 secret when the United States is aggressively trying to sell the aircraft abroad. 
We do not yet fully understand whether this was an innocent (if catastrophic) error, or if it was the result of a complex and successful Chinese espionage operation. If the latter, we don’t know if Chinese intelligence has been able to exploit the shipment, though it appears that Beijing is in possession of the errant parts. But even if the diversion of the shipment to Hong Kong was accidental and not part of an espionage operation, the incident highlights some of the contradictions inherent in the F-35 program.
The F-35 is a supremely advanced fighter aircraft with many proprietary components that would be of immense value to several foreign intelligence services. It is also a consumer product that the United States has been trying to aggressively export over the past two decades to most every country in the Global North and a few in the Global South. Jonathan Caverley has called the F-35 “America’s Belt and Road,” because of both its substantial expense and because of its integrated production over several countries and integrated maintenance over several more. Work in all of these countries is spread among dozens of contractors and subcontractors, each of which offers a potential weak link in terms of keeping the parts of the aircraft secret and secure. 
There are a limited number of countries that could usefully exploit the technology in the shipment, and China is one of them. Of particular concern is the canopy, which represents an enormous technological and financial investment and which could conceivably benefit China’s aerospace industry. As with most such cases, the issue here is less that Chinese engineers could copy the equipment and then integrate it into their own aircraft (modern industrial aerospace techniques are remarkably complex) but rather that careful study could reveal vulnerabilities or characteristics that could eventually give Chinese pilots a tactical advantage.

articles.title: Burmese Refugees in Thailand Face Fresh Deportation Threat
articles.full_text:
A recently-passed law increases the risk that people fleeing repression will be deported and forcibly recruited into the military’s units of “one-way troops.”
Nway, a Burmese political activist who fled Myanmar to avoid forcible conscription into the military, sits for an interview in Chiang Mai, Thailand, September 2026.
In April of 2026, 23-year-old Nway became scared of the dark for the first time in her life. She would lie awake at night, jumping at the noise of a car engine humming past the house she shared with her single mother, anxious that she could be dragged from her bed as she slept.
Her fear of the dark was not unfounded. As a Burmese political activist who had spent the last four years of her life in prison until April of this year, she was a high-profile target for forced conscription into the Myanmar military, which seized power in a coup in 2021. The military, which now fully controls only around 20 percent of the country’s territory, has conscripted over 30,000 young people since February 2024 in a bid to strengthen their struggling forces.
Since then, young people have been grabbed from the street, their workplaces, and their homes, after which they are reportedly deployed to the frontlines and used as “cannon fodder and human shields.” Nway said that her cousin was abducted by the authorities while drinking with friends by the river in Yangon one evening in 2024. He returned home earlier this year to share that “everyone except him had died; he was the one and only lucky man.”
Nway’s previous activism meant that when she was released from prison, she was targeted by the police, who would sit outside her home and visit her mother weekly to tell her, “if you don’t give us money, she will be listed.” Concerned for her daughter’s safety, Nway’s mother instead paid the authorities for her to fly safely to Thailand. Nway found a community of Burmese refugees and activists in the northern city of Chiang Mai, many of whom had similarly been targeted for conscription before fleeing the country.
Since the military coup, thousands of young refugees like Nway have started to rebuild their lives in Thailand, following in the footsteps of past generations of refugees and exiles. But harassment and arrests from Thai police and a deportation law approved in August continue to threaten their security. The new legal framework has been developed for “administering deportation issues speedily and effectively” in the absence of pre-existing “concrete guidelines.” According to civil society organizations, the new laws are already a source of concern for refugees in Thailand.
When Nway arrived in northern Thailand, she was reunited with Pho Thar, another activist and photojournalist whom she had known at university. Both had been held in separate facilities in Yangon’s Insein Prison for years, reuniting only once they had left the country. Pho Thar has already secured his migrant worker’s card, known as a “pink card,” which is the most accessible way for Myanmar nationals to gain legal residency, and Nway is in the process of securing her own.
Nway and Pho Thar are comfortable sharing their stories and names because they know they can never return to Myanmar. For Nway, this is because an outstanding legal case ensures she will be arrested and likely conscripted. Pho Thar, who has already been arrested four times by the Burmese authorities, believes he will be killed if he returns. Sitting outside a Burmese-owned restaurant on the edge of the city, he cracks his shoulder, a permanent injury sustained during his last arrest.
When Pho Thar was released from prison in November 2025, he knew he was listed for conscription and left Yangon within five days, travelling to Karen State where friends in the People’s Defense Forces helped him cross the border.
Pho Thar decided to travel straight to Chiang Mai when he entered Thailand because he believed the risk of staying in the border city of Mae Sot without documentation would be too high. Almost half of the nearly 4 million Myanmar nationals living in Thailand are undocumented and they face regular harassment, extortion, and threats of deportation from the Thai authorities. A 2025 report by Human Rights Watch (HRW) identified that police bribes had become so prevalent in Mae Sot that they referred to Myanmar nationals as “walking ATMs.”
Fear of the authorities and deportation has ruled the lives of several young Burmese refugees who agreed to speak to The Diplomat on condition of anonymity.
One 22-year-old Burmese refugee, Aung*, said that as an undocumented migrant, he found work in a garment factory where he is paid only 150 baht a day – the equivalent of around $4.50 and below minimum wage – and receives one day off per month. Despite his exhaustion, he is grateful for the layer of protection this workplace provides from the police. “I’m always afraid of the Thai police so I rarely go out to the town, I always stay in my factory,” he said.
In Myanmar, the parents of young people who have fled the country continue to pay bribes to Burmese authorities so their other children are not conscripted instead. Aung said that until August 2026, his mother continued to pay for him. “If I was deported to Myanmar, I would be taken to the frontlines and I will never go back home,” he said. “I face difficulty in Mae Sot so I always miss my home. I want to go back, but it is not possible.”
Thirty-five-year-old music producer Kyaw* also said that his mother, who recently recovered from breast cancer, continues to pay monthly bribes for her three children who have fled the country. He is still waiting for his documents in Mae Sot, and similarly knows that if he was deported he would be forced to join what he calls the “one-way troops” that are sent to the frontlines. He decided to leave Yangon when he went to the smoking area near his workplace and witnessed several young colleagues being kidnapped by military personnel during a work break.
Having already paid a 14-million-kyat bribe – over $6,600 – after being arbitrarily arrested and threatened with conscription, Kyaw started the long journey to the border. “I didn’t want to serve in the military because it’s just a civil war,” he said. “Since moving to Thailand, I have to start from zero but if I don’t have anything to eat I don’t care; I will sing a song for the revolution.”
Elsa, who fled to Mae Sot in 2023 with her family, said that they had to wait until 2025 for them to receive their migrant worker’s cards. She reported that they did not leave their home for four months between April and August in 2024 due to increased patrols and arrests by the authorities. She now works in an office but said that “it is a difficult life.”
Since Thai immigration laws do not recognize Myanmar nationals as refugees, and Thailand has not signed the 1951 Refugee Convention, the paths to residency are limited and refugees rely on a broker to navigate the application process for a worker’s card. Interviewees in HRW’s report confirmed that it was unclear exactly what the fees they were paying brokers were being used for in the application process.
In late August, new deportation regulations were approved by the Thai government, which facilitate the prompt deportation of “undesirable” foreigners. Civil society organizations have criticized this legislation, calling for it to include safeguards protecting refugees from deportation. As it stands, while the legislation acknowledges decisions around deportation should account for Thailand’s “relevant international obligations” there is no mention of non-refoulement, which would prevent refugees or asylum seekers from being sent back to any country where they could face persecution or serious harm.
Two foreign nationals have already been deported under the new legal framework. Thanida Piyachot, a human rights specialist at the advocacy group Fortify Rights, said that “the Thai government’s enactment of regulations that can directly affect people’s rights without a thorough review is already deeply concerning. Now, with the enforcement of this fast-track deportation process, serious questions remain about how decisions will be made in practice when there are no clear standards of safeguards.”
Tanyakorn Thippayapokin, the policy, advocacy, and communications coordinator at Asylum Access Thailand, added that it’s very likely the law will be used to extort, harass, and deport Burmese nationals because it is written “very broadly to target anyone staying illegally in the country.”
The Coalition for the Rights of Refugees and Stateless Persons, which includes Fortify Rights and Asylum Access, has called for the government to promptly review the regulations with civil society organizations to address gaps that could put refugees at risk of forced returns and have a standard operating procedure that aligns with principles of non-refoulement.
For the undocumented refugees who are waiting for their migrant worker’s card applications to be processed, this law adds to their concerns about being deported to Myanmar and forcibly recruited. Everyone interviewed by The Diplomat believed that deportation would result in them being conscripted against their will and likely dying on the frontlines, a risk that does not appear to have been considered under this new legal framework, according to civil society organizations.
Piyachot argued that the new law is already impacting the security of undocumented Burmese migrants. “It is creating fear among refugee communities. I believe [the authorities] can use this law to threaten them, and worsen the corruption and extortion,” she said.
Meanwhile, Nway is trying to start a new life in Chiang Mai, alongside Pho Thar. Now she is in Thailand, she says she “doesn’t expect a lot. I really want to go back to my country because it’s where my childhood memories are, but it’s impossible.”
Instead, she says she wants a simple life. “I don’t want to worry again about what will happen at night, like in Yangon,” Nway said. “I want to sleep peacefully.”
*Some names have been changed to preserve respondents’ anonymity.
In April of 2026, 23-year-old Nway became scared of the dark for the first time in her life. She would lie awake at night, jumping at the noise of a car engine humming past the house she shared with her single mother, anxious that she could be dragged from her bed as she slept.
Her fear of the dark was not unfounded. As a Burmese political activist who had spent the last four years of her life in prison until April of this year, she was a high-profile target for forced conscription into the Myanmar military, which seized power in a coup in 2021. The military, which now fully controls only around 20 percent of the country’s territory, has conscripted over 30,000 young people since February 2024 in a bid to strengthen their struggling forces.
Since then, young people have been grabbed from the street, their workplaces, and their homes, after which they are reportedly deployed to the frontlines and used as “cannon fodder and human shields.” Nway said that her cousin was abducted by the authorities while drinking with friends by the river in Yangon one evening in 2024. He returned home earlier this year to share that “everyone except him had died; he was the one and only lucky man.”

articles.title: 166 Civil Society Groups Urge Halt to Malaysia’s Rohingya Deportation Plan
articles.full_text:
The organizations expressed “grave concern” about the repatriation of refugees to Myanmar, citing the risks of violent persecution and forced conscription.
Two elderly Rohingya refugees at their home in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
More than 160 civil society organizations yesterday urged Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim to halt plans to deport ​Rohingya refugees to Myanmar, saying that they could face severe risks including ongoing violence ‌and forced conscription into the military.
Last week, Anwar said that he planned to invite military-appointed leader Min Aung Hlaing to Malaysia, in a bid to expedite the repatriation of tens of thousands of Rohingya Muslims who have sought sanctuary in Malaysia over the past decade.
Anwar’s government has already reached a deal with Naypyidaw for the “voluntary” repatriation of some 5,000 refugees, which make up around half of the 10,388 Myanmar nationals currently being held at the country’s immigration detention depots. The first 1,476 of this group is scheduled to return to Myanmar on September 29 aboard two Myanmar Navy warships and a hospital ship.
In their statement, the civil society groups, which included both Malaysian, Myanmar, and international organizations, expressed “grave concern” about the planned deportations, contrasting Malaysia’s treatment of the Rohingya with its vocal advocacy of the Palestinian cause. They also lambasted Anwar’s willingness to roll out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing.
“Malaysia’s engagement with the junta must not come at the expense of its own reputation and integrity. Cozying up to genocidaires while criminalizing their survivors is not only illogical but also immoral,” the groups said. “Refoulement of the Rohingya by Malaysia or any ASEAN member state will make them complicit in the ongoing genocide of the Rohingya.”
In their statement, the civil society groups pointed to the continuing conflict in Rakhine State, the home of most Rohingya refugees. It also pointed to a pattern of forced conscription of Rohingya populations by the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army (AA), a Rakhine nationalist armed group that now controls the majority of Rakhine.
The groups called for an “immediate halt” to the planned deportations of all Myanmar nationals, pending a “comprehensive assessment of the situation” in the country.
“Sending Rohingya into a situation of forced conscription will prolong and intensify rather than reduce the conflict,” it stated.
Large numbers of Rohingya have flowed into Malaysian since 2017, when the Myanmar military launched an ethnic cleansing campaign that pushed more than 740,000 from their homes in Rakhine State into Bangladesh. As of February, 193,800 refugees from Myanmar were registered with the U.N. refugee agency in Kuala Lumpur, of which 126,000 were Rohingya. Malaysia does not recognize any of them as refugees.
In recent months, Anwar has come under growing pressure to respond a tide of public hostility toward the Rohingya in Malaysia, which has been marked by an upsurge of xenophobic rhetoric, particularly online, and inflammatory comments by prominent public figures, who have described the Rohingya as “criminals” and “intruders” and likened them to a “cancer” on the country. Across the country, Rohingya refugee schools ​have been forced to close due to harassment and ⁠threats.
Among ASEAN governments, Malaysia has been among the most critical of the Myanmar military’s seizure of power in 2021, and its ruthless attempts to put down the armed uprising that followed. But the growing domestic pressure over refugees has forced Anwar to adopt a more accommodating position toward Naypyidaw.
In a podcast interview last week, he announced plans to invite Min Aung Hlaing to undertake an official visit to Malaysia, which would make it the fifth ASEAN member state to welcome the coup leader since he was elected president by Myanmar’s military-dominated parliament in April. Anwar said that Malaysia was not ready to recognize the government, ⁠but needed an authority to negotiate with on returning refugees.
“I invited him to say we can be friends, ​we can trade, we can accept Myanmar, but Myanmar must accept them [the refugees] back,” he said. “Otherwise, this will continue to place a burden on security, and the economy, while also creating tensions among the public.”
This language was echoed by the Ministry of Home Affairs in its announcement of the September 29 deportation, when it said that the refugees’ presence had become a “major financial burden, caused serious social problems, and created a real security threat to the country.”
In their statement, civil society groups said that this campaign appeared to be “a cynical tactic” by politicians aimed at ginning up support ahead of the next Malaysian general election, which is due to be held by 2028.
