articles.title: Rare Earths at the Trump-Xi Summit: Relief Without a Resolution
articles.full_text:
The Trump-Xi meeting may temporarily ease anxiety over rare earth supplies, but it is unlikely to lower the political and regulatory threshold for access.
Rare earths entered the Trump-Xi summit before the two leaders even sat down. On September 21, two days before President Xi Jinping’s arrival in the United States, China’s Foreign Ministry faced a series of questions on whether Beijing had “fully resumed rare earth deliveries,” whether a “November 10 deadline or expanded restrictions on rare earth exports” could be extended, and whether rare earths controls involving Japan would feature in the Washington talks. The responses were deliberately cautious: Beijing reiterated its commitment to “keeping the global industrial and supply chains of critical minerals safe and stable,” but emphasized that dual-use exports would remain subject to legal and security considerations. 
The Foreign Ministry’s responses captured the central paradox of the summit: it may temporarily ease anxiety over rare earth supplies, but it is unlikely to lower the political and regulatory threshold for access.
In April 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce and General Administration of Customs placed several medium and heavy rare earth elements – including samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, and yttrium – under export controls. Exporters of these items are required to apply for licenses, with the stated legal basis including China’s Export Control Law and regulations on dual-use items. This does not amount to a blanket ban on exports, but it does shift rare earth access from a purely commercial transaction to a regulated process shaped by licensing, end-use review, and national security considerations. Once such controls are embedded in a legal and bureaucratic system, they are not easily removed. A summit can improve predictability, but it will not result in the dismantling of China’s carefully built legal framework for export controls.
The same logic applies on the U.S. side. Even if the summit reduces short-term pressure, Washington is unlikely to abandon its effort to diversify away from China-centered critical mineral supply chains. In January 2026, the White House framed U.S. dependence on imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products as a national security concern, noting that even where the United States has domestic mining capacity, it often lacks sufficient downstream processing capacity. The policy response has therefore gone beyond asking China for more predictable deliveries. The United States is investing in domestic processing, recycling and alternative supply chains, while also working with allies and partners to reduce exposure to single-source dependence. In this sense, any relief produced by the summit may buy some time, but it will not weaken Washington’s broader push for supply-chain diversification.
Rare earths occupy this strategic space because they are not simply another category of traded minerals. Their importance lies less in the raw materials themselves than in the capabilities of the downstream industries they support: high-performance magnets, electric vehicles, wind turbines, advanced electronics and defense systems. This gives rare earths a dual character. They are commercial inputs for global industries, but they are also strategic enablers for military and technological power. 
Once a commodity acquires this dual-use profile, access to it is unlikely to be governed by market logic alone. For China, this strengthens the case for licensing and end-use scrutiny. For the United States, it reinforces the argument that dependence on China-centered supply chains is not merely an economic risk, but a strategic vulnerability. China does not control every part of the global rare earth supply chain, but its position in processing and export licensing gives it a more immediate ability to shape access. This mismatch between China’s immediate leverage and the United States’ long-term adjustment capacity creates bargaining space, but not enough for a full reset. articles.title: Will the World Ever Take Action on Myanmar?
articles.full_text:
The evidence of atrocities is there. What are governments prepared to do with that knowledge?
The Human Rights and Alliance of Civilizations Room at the United Nations’ Geneva headquarters, which houses the United Nations Human Rights Council.
We came to Geneva for the 63rd Human Rights Council from different points in our advocacy journeys and different parts of the world, but with a shared commitment to the people of Myanmar. One of us has spent years walking the corridors of the United Nations, meeting diplomats, and pressing governments to act on the crisis in Myanmar. The other was attending the Human Rights Council for the first time, after years of documenting human rights violations in the country.
We were there for the same reason: to ask governments what they are prepared to do about Myanmar. After years of documenting atrocities, we left Geneva with a question that is becoming increasingly difficult to avoid: what happens when the evidence is already there?
Inside the Human Rights Council chamber, the scale of the crisis was once again laid bare.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, described a deepening crisis marked by attacks by the military junta, including airstrikes, forced conscription, arbitrary detention, sexual violence, displacement, and the weaponization of humanitarian assistance. He urged United Nations member states to refer the situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court through the Security Council and halt transfers of arms, ammunition, jet fuel, and dual-use items that risk facilitating violations of international law.
The head of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, Nicholas Koumjian, reported that serious international crimes are being committed with greater frequency and intensity. The mechanism is continuing to collect and preserve evidence for future accountability.
At HRC63, we heard a wide range of approaches to the crisis in Myanmar.
Of the 39 governments and entities that took the floor, fewer than half – just 14 – explicitly raised accountability, justice, impunity, or international accountability mechanisms. While 20 speakers expressed broad support for stronger action, the rest of the room fragmented: eight, including Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, India, and Vietnam, appeared supportive but cautious, favoring regional engagement, dialogue, and a “Myanmar-owned or Myanmar-led” process.
Five governments – Laos, Belarus, Russia, China, and Venezuela – actively shielded the regime, emphasizing sovereignty, non-interference, and engagement with Myanmar’s authorities, while opposing international pressure.
After the session, we met with several diplomatic missions in Geneva. For us, these meetings created space for conversations about what more can be done. What we heard in the Council and in those meetings was not a lack of awareness. Myanmar is simply not a sufficiently high political priority for many governments to generate sustained action.
There are real diplomatic complications. Myanmar’s political representation remains contested, including at the United Nations, where the question of who represents the country remains unresolved. Governments also have different relationships with the military junta, the National Unity Government, ethnic resistance organizations, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). But these complications cannot be grounds for indefinite inaction and impunity.
In our view, a Myanmar-led or ASEAN-led process should have a major role. Humanitarian assistance is essential. But none of these should mean putting accountability or the protection of civilians on hold.
Dialogue with a brutal regime cannot become a substitute for accountability, and sovereignty cannot serve as a shield against international scrutiny.
Human rights defenders, within Myanmar and outside, are still doing their part. We continue to document violations, speak with survivors, share evidence with the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, and engage with the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Other Myanmar and regional organizations are doing the same.
Fortify Rights has documented the military’s aerial attacks on civilians, including the chain of command behind attacks in Kachin and Karenni states, and has continued to record new methods of aerial warfare.
Although more documentation is needed, what is missing is a comparable machinery of political action. 
Some governments are already using some of the tools available to them. Canada maintains an arms embargo and aviation-fuel prohibition and has continued imposing targeted sanctions on Myanmar military officials and entities. The United Kingdom and the European Union have also imposed sanctions targeting aviation fuel suppliers and other entities linked to the military. 
At the same time, accountability efforts are moving forward. Myanmar and Rohingya organizations have pursued universal-jurisdiction cases in Argentina, Germany, Indonesia, the Philippines, Timor-Leste, and Turkiye. In November 2024, the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing, while in January 2026, the International Court of Justice held merits hearings in The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar.
And yet, from where we sit, there is still a striking gap between the evidence being gathered and meaningful accountability for crimes committed since the 2021 coup. No international court is currently prosecuting the full range of those crimes. National cases and international proceedings offer important pathways, but they do not yet amount to a comprehensive accountability process.
What stayed with us from the 63rd Human Rights Council was not a lack of information or evidence. The evidence is being collected, and governments should continue to fund human rights documentation. Cases are being pursued. Some governments are taking action. But the pieces are still not coming together at the scale needed to match the crisis.
We can continue to document, share evidence, and engage governments. But documentation can only go so far without political action. The people of Myanmar have been waiting for years, and the evidence is there. What happens next depends on what governments do with it.

articles.title: Xi Jinping Is Coming to the US. Why Is He Skipping the UNGA?
articles.full_text:
Xi’s coming to the U.S. East Coast while the United Nations’ biggest event is going on. That makes his absence all the more striking.
Chinese President Xi Jinping addresses the general debate of the General Assembly’s 70th session, Sep. 28, 2015. That was the first and only time Xi attended a session of the UNGA in person.
If you read The Diplomat, you probably follow Asia-Pacific affairs – and thus you probably already know that Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to arrive in Washington, D.C. today for a much-anticipated summit with U.S. President Donald Trump.
According to the White House’s itinerary, Xi will land at Andrews Air Force Base on September 23, where he will be personally received by Trump himself. The next day, he’ll receive a formal welcome ceremony at the White House, followed by the actual summit and a state dinner. On September 25, Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will host Xi and his wife for tea; both couples will then visit the National Archives, “where they will view a variety of important records and documents significant to the American and Chinese relationship throughout history.” Then Xi and his delegation will fly home.
What’s most remarkable about this itinerary is what it doesn’t include: a stop in New York, where the United Nations’ General Assembly is currently holding its 81st session. Heads of state and government from around the world are making the trip to New York just for the UNGA, including top leaders from Bangladesh, Japan, Indonesia, Kyrgyzstan, Nepal, Mongolia, South Korea, and Vietnam, just to name a few from The Diplomat’s coverage region.
Meanwhile, Xi is making a trip across the Pacific Ocean and the entire continental U.S. and not bothering to take an extra jaunt up the coast to attend the United Nations’ most important annual event.
Instead, Vice President Han Zheng will be in New York from September 24 to 26 to represent China at the UNGA. According to China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, “On the sidelines of the general debate, Vice President Han will attend the High-Level Dialogue on the Fifth Anniversary of the Global Development Initiative hosted by China, and meet with [the] U.N. secretary-general, president of the 81st UNGA session, and leaders of relevant countries.”
Apparently, these are meetings Xi couldn’t be bothered to attend himself, despite being just an hour’s plane ride away. 
Xi’s absence from the UNGA would seem to undermine China’s consistent rhetorical emphasis on the United Nations’ importance. China’s white paper on global governance, released in June 2026, repeatedly emphasized the U.N. as the “core” of the international  order. “The United Nations is the primary platform for practicing multilateralism and advancing global governance,” the white paper declared. “Its leading position must be upheld and remain rock solid; its role can only be reinforced, not weakened.”
In the same press conference where Guo announced Han’s trip, the spokesperson repeated a similar line: “The United Nations is the core platform for global governance, and the general debate of UNGA is a vital opportunity for countries to build political consensus and coordinate multilateral actions.” But if the United Nations, and the UNGA, are so important, why can’t Xi be bothered to attend?
Xi has gone to the UNGA just once since becoming China’s top leader in late 2012. He went in 2015, to commemorate the United Nations’ 70th anniversary, and addressed the UNGA in person for the first and only time.
Notably, this coincided with Xi’s last state visit to the United States, when he included attendance at the UNGA within a broader itinerary that saw him also hold a summit with then-U.S. President Barack Obama. That makes the decision not to do the same thing in 2026 all the more notable.
In 2021, Xi gave a video address to the UNGA, in which he announced China’s Global Development Initiative. He has not delivered a speech before the UNGA since.
Perhaps most notably, Xi chose to skip last year’s UNGA – the 80th session. China puts much stock in these round-number anniversaries, pegging trips abroad and major upgrades in bilateral relations to special dates. Remember that Xi took the time to attend the United Nations’ 70th anniversary in person. That wasn’t an aberration – China’s top leader had attended every decennial anniversary of the U.N. since Jiang Zemin in 1995. That made Xi’s absence from the 80th anniversary in 2025 all the more conspicuous. 
Instead [of attending the UNGA], Xi stayed in China, where he “extended festive greetings” for the farmers’ harvest celebration and visited Urumqi to mark the 70th anniversary of the founding of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
Those events were duly splashed across the front-page headlines of People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party. Premier Li Qiang’s presence at UNGA received just a one-line mention on the front page for September 24.
Xi has also stopped announcing China’s major global initiatives at the United Nations. He unveiled the Global Development Initiative at the UNGA back in 2021, albeit in a virtual speech. But in 2025, Xi chose to announce the new Global Governance Initiative – even more directly related to the United Nations’ mission – at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit held in China a month before the UNGA.
Similarly, China founded its own World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) – “an independent intergovernmental international organization that… aims to promote international cooperation and global governance on artificial intelligence” – rather than working within the United Nations to legitimize its efforts toward the same ends. China announced WAICO at its own AI conference, rather than at the U.N. Global Dialogue on AI Governance held a month earlier.
Meanwhile, as Trump reduces U.S. funding for the United Nations, China hasn’t stepped up to fill the gap. Its own U.N.-assessed contributions have been chronically late and remain a mere fraction of what the United States was contributing prior to Trump taking office.
No matter the lip service China pays to the United Nations’ “core role” in global governance, Beijing clearly prefers to give attention, money, and prestige to settings where it exerts more control. That includes China-led groups like the SCO, but also purely bilateral meetings like the summit with Trump. 
Nikkei Asia theorized that Xi’s decision to skip the UNGA was an attempt to position China as a true equal to the United States – a message that apparently would have been diluted by Xi rubbing elbows with leaders from smaller states in New York. That in itself is telling. For all China’s rhetoric about a multipolar world where all states have equal representation – and equal say – in global governance, when push comes to shove Beijing defaults to a different perspective.
As China’s top diplomat put it, fairly undiplomatically, in a heated ASEAN meeting back in 2010: “China is a big country and other countries are small countries, and that’s just a fact.” One of the perks of being a “big country,” as Trump has repeatedly shown, is the privilege of ignoring the United Nations to pursue national interests in other settings.

articles.title: On Taiwan, US ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Is Not Dead Yet
articles.full_text:
What look like indications of U.S. abandonment of Taiwan are relatively superficial, while substantive investment in capabilities that could deter China continues apace.
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks at a press conference at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, Jan. 3, 2026.
Under the longstanding policy of “strategic ambiguity,” the U.S. government has refused to say ahead of time whether or not it would send American forces to help defend Taiwan against an attack from China. Some analysts say the Trump administration has rendered this policy ineffective by generating doubt that U.S. forces would intervene.
To cite just one example, the title of a September 14 analysis by columnist James Crabtree in Foreign Policy proclaimed that “Trump is killing ‘strategic ambiguity’ over Taiwan.” Crabtree argued that based on “signals from Washington,” the United States is “inching more toward a position of nonintervention.” Similarly, geopolitical risk analyst Shahn Louis said “the era” of strategic ambiguity “is over.”  Michael Schiffer, a former U.S. deputy assistant secretary of defense for East Asia, argued that “strategic ambiguity is no longer a sustainable or effective policy.” 
Multiple opinion polls show the belief among Taiwan’s people that the United States would ride to the rescue has decreased since 2025. The reasons for this loss of credibility are not hard to find.
Trump has repeatedly made four points about Taiwan, all of which call into question a robust U.S. response to military action by Beijing. The first is that Taiwan is vastly smaller and less important than China. Second, he says Taiwan is indefensible – too close to China and far from the United States. Third, Trump thinks Taiwan free-rides on U.S. defense. Finally, he complains about Taiwan allegedly stealing America’s semiconductor industry. Shortly before he took office for the second time, Trump said he would respond to a Chinese invasion of Taiwan with economic sanctions.
On top of this, Trump avoids antagonizing Beijing over the Taiwan issue, presumably to clear the way for a China-U.S. bilateral economic deal. During his keynote speech at the 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not mention Taiwan, a change from his speech the previous year. The unclassified version of the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy also does not mention Taiwan by name.
After his May 2026 meeting with Xi Jinping, Trump criticized the Taiwan government for allegedly flirting with independence due to the presumption of U.S. support. “[W]e’re not looking to have somebody say, ‘Let’s go independent because the United States is backing us,’” he told Fox News.
For good measure, Trump announced that he was delaying a large arms sale to Taiwan already approved by Congress, calling such sales a “very good negotiating chip” in talks with China. He also dismissed the Six Assurances, part of U.S. policy toward Taiwan since the Reagan era. 
The idea that strategic ambiguity has lost its usefulness, however, is wrong. Despite particular statements by Trump that are adverse to Taiwan, U.S. policy remains broadly supportive of Taipei. 
The Pentagon’s 2026 National Defense Strategy said the United States will “erect” and “sustain a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain.” Even a cursory look at a map indicates that aspiration is meaningless without a U.S. intent to prevent China from absorbing Taiwan. 
The large arms sale is delayed, but not canceled. This latest package of armaments is all business, not symbolic. It includes weapons systems appropriate for the scenario of an attempted amphibious invasion by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA): HIMARS rockets, ATACMS missiles, ALTIUS loitering munition drones, Javelin and TOW anti-tank missiles, and mobile howitzers.
U.S. military transits through the Taiwan Strait continue, albeit about half as often as during Trump’s first term.
U.S. security cooperation with the Philippines and Japan, highly relevant to deterring China from moving aggressively against Taiwan, has deepened during the second Trump administration.
The United States got access to, and set aside funding to develop infrastructure in, additional base sites in the northern Philippines, close to the Taiwan Strait. The annual Balikatan military exercises were larger than ever before in 2025 and 2026 and brought in Japan and Australia. U.S. forces deployed NMESIS and Typhon missile systems to the Philippines. The stridency of China’s complaints about these deployments indicate they present problems for Chinese planners.
Washington’s plan to upgrade U.S. Forces Japan to a joint force combat headquarters has proceeded under Trump’s second administration. U.S. and Japanese armed forces increased their interoperability in 2025 and 2026 through more integrated command-and-control structures, more complex joint exercises, and more sharing of data. The United States started supplying Tomahawk cruise missiles to Japan. Washington and Tokyo are engaged in serious discussions about Japan producing warships or components for the U.S. Navy to help it close the gap with China’s production. 
Strategic ambiguity still holds because what look like indications of U.S. abandonment of Taiwan are relatively superficial, while substantive investment in capabilities that could deter China continues apace.
The stances of the Joe Biden presidency and the second Trump administration are different. Biden said on four occasions that the United States would militarily intervene in a cross-strait war, placing him close to an unambiguous pre-commitment to intervention. Trump is closer to the other end, a pre-commitment to non-intervention.
Both, however, represent forms of strategic ambiguity. One president seemed committed and the other reluctant, but who knows what either of them would actually decide to do at crunch time. Beijing still cannot confidently assume a Trump-led United States would not intervene in a Taiwan scenario despite Trump seemingly indicating reticence to do so.
Chinese analysts consider Trump to be unpredictable. They cannot be sure he will act in a way consistent with his past statements.  The Chinese remember how quickly Trump turned on them in 2020. In January, he said “our relationship with China now might be the best it’s been in a long, long time.” Later in the year, largely over the COVID-19 pandemic, Trump regularly berated China with statements such as “I’m very angry at China” and “The world is now suffering as a result of the malfeasance of the Chinese government.”
There are, nevertheless, reasons to doubt the American commitment to defend Taiwan, and these reasons go beyond the current U.S. presidential administration.
First, the demographic trend in the United States is increasingly anti-war. Gen Z Americans, born 1997-2012, are significantly less fearful of China attaining a stronger global position and less likely to see China as an adversary. The succession of unpopular wars against Afghanistan, Iraq and Iran further strengthens the aversion of Americans toward getting embroiled in foreign conflicts.
Second, the costs and risks of maintaining U.S. strategic pre-eminence on the western Pacific Rim against the determination of China to achieve regional supremacy are rising. The United States already dominates the Western Hemisphere. The rationale for dominating the Asia-Pacific, as well, is that doing so makes war less likely and opens the door for U.S. commerce. This rationale is less persuasive, however, if China supports international trade and if opposing China’s aspirations for “rejuvenation” makes war more rather than less likely.
Military analyst Jennifer Kavanaugh’s September 10 proposal for a “Second Island Chain strategy” attracted much attention. Kavanaugh, a member of the “restrainer” camp in U.S. foreign policy, argued that to reduce the risk of war with China while still protecting the most vital U.S. interests, Washington should end its alliances with Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the Philippines, pull most of its military forces out of the region, and announce that it will not intervene to protect Taiwan in a cross-strait war. Expect arguments such as this to grow in volume and frequency.
Finally, the U.S. defense industrial base is currently unable to compete with China’s productivity. This weakness is not easily fixed, even with an increased defense budget. As the modernization of its armed forces have made China a near-peer adversary of the United States, China’s advantage in manufacturing capacity becomes potentially decisive in a theoretical China-U.S. war.  
Recent wargaming suggests both China and the U.S. would suffer huge losses in a conflict. Even where the U.S. “wins,” China is better placed to quickly rebuild and rearm its forces, giving Beijing hope that it would prevail in a second round. If American leaders conclude the math leaves them without a path to victory, they will reconsider whether an intervention is feasible. 
But for now, Beijing would be reckless not to assume that both the United States and Japan would militarily oppose an attempt to conquer Taiwan. And Xi is not reckless.
Under the longstanding policy of “strategic ambiguity,” the U.S. government has refused to say ahead of time whether or not it would send American forces to help defend Taiwan against an attack from China. Some analysts say the Trump administration has rendered this policy ineffective by generating doubt that U.S. forces would intervene.
To cite just one example, the title of a September 14 analysis by columnist James Crabtree in Foreign Policy proclaimed that “Trump is killing ‘strategic ambiguity’ over Taiwan.” Crabtree argued that based on “signals from Washington,” the United States is “inching more toward a position of nonintervention.” Similarly, geopolitical risk analyst Shahn Louis said “the era” of strategic ambiguity “is over.”  Michael Schiffer, a former U.S. deputy assistant secretary of defense for East Asia, argued that “strategic ambiguity is no longer a sustainable or effective policy.” 
Multiple opinion polls show the belief among Taiwan’s people that the United States would ride to the rescue has decreased since 2025. The reasons for this loss of credibility are not hard to find.
articles.summary: What look like indications of U.S. abandonment of Taiwan are relatively superficial, while substantive investment in capabilities that could deter China continues apace.

articles.title: The Trump-Xi Summit: Stakes for Australia
articles.full_text:
Trump wants more sales. Xi wants fewer constraints. What does Australia need from the Trump-Xi summit?
U.S. President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping before a bilateral meeting at the Gimhae International Airport terminal in Busan, South Korea, Oct. 30, 2025.
Chinese media have confirmed that Xi Jinping will make a state visit to Washington from September 23 to 25 for a much-anticipated summit with U.S. President Donald Trump. The announcement followed talks between their economic chiefs in New York on September 20. 
Although the two sides have framed those discussions differently, it is clear that trade and AI will be on the summit agenda. Trump could leave with more orders, Xi with fewer constraints on China’s technological development, and both declare success. For Canberra, the question is what their bargain would mean for Australian investments and security arrangements built around sustained China-U.S. competition.
Allied unease is already visible. On September 21, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Japanese and South Korean counterparts in New York. Their joint statement reiterated the United States’ “ironclad” defence commitments, opposed economic coercion, and stressed peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae secured a meeting with Trump on September 22, just before the summit, while South Korean President Lee Jae-myung sought contact during the United Nations General Assembly. Tokyo and Seoul want their security and economic concerns heard before Trump meets Xi. Canberra should draw the same lesson.
Like the Trump-Xi summit held in Beijing in May, this one is likely to buy time rather than lasting stability. The deadline that matters for business falls around November 10. Three temporary arrangements approach their expiration date: Washington’s suspension of restrictions on majority-owned affiliates of listed entities, China’s suspension of expanded rare earth and related export controls, and 178 U.S. tariff exclusions for Chinese goods. The practical questions are how long these pauses will be extended and on what terms.
Trump wants commercial wins ahead of the midterms. Xi wants fewer constraints on China’s technological development. Trade concessions can serve both purposes without resolving the contest over power in the digital age.
Trade and technology may therefore move in different directions. Tariff relief and purchase commitments could coexist with tighter restrictions on advanced chips and overseas computing access. Xi cannot assume Trump can trade these restrictions away. They have bipartisan support in Congress and deep backing in the Pentagon and Commerce Department. 
Beijing increasingly treats efforts to block its technological advance as a challenge to its right to development, one of the four red lines in Xi’s book. It will resist broader technology restrictions and pressure on third countries to choose sides.
The two leaders have different philosophies of negotiation. Trump assumes that, at the right price, almost any arrangement can be renegotiated. Xi allows for pragmatism and ambiguity within fixed limits. Beijing accepts broadly worded commitments but demands clarity on Taiwan and its political system. Washington insists on verifiable trade commitments while deliberately leaving uncertain whether it would intervene militarily over Taiwan. Both leaders have domestic reasons to compromise, but both may sign the same wording and mean different things.
Australia has to plan for the consequences. Canberra should compare their announcements for differences in scope, duration, and conditions before treating a diplomatic statement as a reliable basis for the future.
The Albanese government has spent years restoring normal trade with China while supporting Washington’s efforts to reduce dependence on it. If Trump and Xi compromise with one another, Australia could be left bearing the costs of reducing dependence on China while Washington negotiates exceptions for itself.
Canberra should seek durable support for mineral projects, cooperation on shared AI risks, and security commitments that survive a bargain with Beijing.
First, critical minerals offer one test. The Australia-U.S. framework envisages price support and financing to develop alternatives to Chinese supply. If Washington and Beijing extend their rare earth arrangements, Canberra should seek assurances that support for Australian alternatives will endure. Australian projects need dependable financing and long-term customers, even when Chinese supplies become easier to obtain.
Second, AI risks extend beyond chips and data centers. Australian businesses use software and digital services shared across borders. Canberra should therefore press for an agreement to warn affected countries and operators of serious AI incidents while there is still time to contain them. Building more local data centers would not, by itself, remove those shared dependencies.
Government hotlines alone cannot do this: the first warning may come from a developer, cloud provider, or independent researcher. Those warnings need to reach Australian authorities and affected businesses without waiting for governments to establish blame. That would give Australia something a bilateral technology deal cannot guarantee: timely notice of a failure that could spread into its own economy. The test is whether warnings reach those who must act, rather than whether the leaders agree to keep talking.
Finally, Australia needs maritime security. Defense-commissioned research reported in 2022 found that a major regional conflict would threaten routes supplying 90 percent of Australia’s refined-fuel imports. With disruption in the Strait of Hormuz already imposing costs, Australia can ill afford another obstructed route in the South China Sea.
Canberra should seek consultation before Washington negotiates any changes affecting its regional military presence or commitments under AUKUS. It should also press for functioning military hotlines and arrangements for reporting incidents at sea and in the air. These mechanisms need procedures both sides will use when tensions rise.
Reaffirming that decisions to use nuclear weapons must remain under human control at the summit would provide another practical safeguard.
Canberra’s test is whether the summit leaves Australia better able to invest, keep essential services running, and protect its trade routes. That requires commitments Washington will honor and crisis arrangements both powers will use. If Trump and Xi buy themselves time while Australia is left carrying the uncertainty, their success will not be ours.

articles.title: At UNGA, Kyrgyz President Japarov Once Again Complains About Sanctions
articles.full_text:
Japarov also thanked Donald Trump for ending funding of NGOs.
Amid his 20-minute remarks before the United Nations General Assembly this week, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov took time to complain about sanctions and thank U.S. President Donald Trump for ceasing support to NGOs.
“…[T]oday sanctions are, in some cases, used by individual countries as an instrument of interference in the internal affairs of sovereign states,” Japarov said. “The negative consequences of unjustified unilateral sanctions also affect small countries such as ours, which are at the stage of formation and development, and this raises concern among other small states as well.”
Japarov went on to claim that “some major states, in pursuit of their own interests, put pressure on smaller countries such as Kyrgyzstan, attempting to force them to bargain over certain matters and issuing ultimatums.”
At no point did Japarov lay out specifically what countries he believes are pressuring Kyrgyzstan, and to what end. 
Then, in the middle of his commentary about sanctions, Japarov pivoted to lauding the U.S. president – although the Trump administration has maintained the prior administration’s sanctions on various Kyrgyz entities.
“In this context, I would like to take this opportunity to note the decision made by the President of the United States His Excellency Mr. Donald Trump after taking office to halt funding of non-governmental organizations around the world,” Japarov said. “As a result, interference by NGOs in the internal affairs and policies of developing states has practically ceased.”
For Japarov, the two issues are inextricably linked. Last year at UNGA, he stated that “sanctions imposed on Kyrgyzstan are based on false information spread by certain non-governmental organizations and malicious citizens.”
Japarov has not specified which NGOs or “malicious citizens” have provided this “false information” that supposedly landed Kyrgyz business and banks on sanctions lists. 
In April, Kyrgyzstan’s Bakai Bank won a case in a Belgian commercial court against the Open Dialogue Foundation (ODF) for its publication of reports alleging that the bank was involved in the circumvention of sanctions against Russia. Note that the bank had not been sanctioned. The court classified the NGO as a “commercial enterprise,” opening it to liability as if it were a market competitor. 
As the World Liberty Congress, a global alliance of pro-democracy leaders, said in a statement: “The court required published information to meet a commercial verification standard designed for disputes between market operators, a test that is structurally impossible for any organization working in an authoritarian jurisdiction where access to primary banking records is unavailable.”
Meanwhile, also in April 2026, the EU aimed its “anti-circumvention tool” at Kyrgyzstan, the first country so targeted. In the subsequent months, Kyrgyz authorities pantomimed taking action. In June 2026, two state-owned banks claimed to have ended partnerships with more than 130 clients due to sanctions risks. In August, another round of cut connections was announced. 
However, Kyrgyz authorities have never specified which companies were affected, making it all but impossible to confirm whether companies that present actual sanctions risks have been cut loose.
According to RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk, as of June 2026, 31 companies from Kyrgyzstan were under Western sanctions, including five banks. While three Tajik banks were removed from the EU sanctions list in May, the Kyrgyz banks – such as Keremet Bank, Kapital Bank, Eurasian Savings Bank, and EcoIslamicBank – remain designated by the EU, the U.K., and/or the U.S.
After thanking Trump “for ending the funding of NGOs,” Japarov continued discussing sanctions, arguing that the decision to impose sanctions should “be taken in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and exclusively within the mandate of the Security Council.”
Kyrgyzstan this year won a non-permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council.
Japarov went on to speak of the U.N. in terms that seem divorced from the body’s current hamstrung reality. “Every decision of the United Nations should be implemented without delay. If a state fails to implement such decision and other countries cease cooperation with it, the effectiveness of sanctions will increase,” he argued.
The permanent members of the UNSC – China, Russia, France, the U.K., and the U.S. – stand on diametrically opposed ends of the global order and this has effectively neutered its possible decisiveness – whether on sanctions or anything else. For example, in September 2022, Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution condemning Moscow’s attempted annexation of parts of Ukraine. The U.S. has repeatedly blocked resolutions targeting Israel. China joined Russia earlier this month to veto an effort to extend the mandate of independent experts monitoring sanctions on Iran.
Suggesting that the UNSC become the central clearinghouse for all sanctions is effectively a call for there to be no sanctions, ever.

articles.title: The China-Russia Factor in the Iran War
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Stephen J. Blank – non-resident senior fellow in the Foreign Policy Research Institute’s Eurasia Program and author of numerous publications on Soviet/Russian, U.S., Asian, and European military and foreign policies – is the 527th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
How is China-Russia cooperation supporting Iran’s resistance against U.S. military actions?
Sino-Russian cooperation supports Iran in many ways. Russia is transmitting satellite intelligence about the location and movement of American troops, ships, and aircraft. Iran used this intelligence to strike U.S. bases in Jordan and Saudi Arabia and may also have obtained Russian intelligence to strike at secret CIA installations. 
Second, Moscow is making good Iranian drone losses, having helped Iran restock about 60 percent of its losses, often with improved versions of drones Iran sent to Russia. Russia also gives Iran tactical guidance on drone use, e.g. how many drones Iran should use and should use and from what altitudes it should shoot. Thus, Iran benefits from Russian lessons in Ukraine. 
Third, Russia’s “Caspian Express” has become a major logistical lifeline for Iran. Lastly Russia provides diplomatic support for Iran.
China and possibly Russia are selling Iran shoulder-fired air missile defenses MANPADS. Chinese engines power the Russian drones sent to Iran, which reportedly also incorporate Chinese radio modems and cameras. China also has recently closed a deal to sell Iran supersonic anti-ship missiles with a range up to 290 km to deter or strike U.S. vessels.
Likewise, Chinese entities provide chemical precursors and dual-use items for Iran’s ballistic missile program. Chinese entities are also reportedly loading Iranian vessels with the solid rocket-fuel precursor, sodium perchlorate, and may be preparing to supply spare parts and missile components. Iran also has military-grade access to China’s Beidou satellite navigation system and China has given Iran geospatial intelligence through state-affiliated commercial satellite companies.
What is the strategic calculus for Beijing and Moscow in bolstering Tehran’s position?
Both Russia and China share a common motivation to weaken the U.S. either leading to its defeat or to a protracted war that bleeds U.S. strength, ties it down in the Gulf, and prevents greater military support for Ukraine, Taiwan, and Washington’s Asian and European allies. They also aim to weaken American alliances, damage America’s global standing and economy, and increase its domestic polarization. Moreover, this war validates their ideology about the decline of an American-led world order and the alleged rise of a new multipolar order, thereby lending credence to that ideology.
How is China benefitting from protracted conflict in both the Ukraine and Iran wars?
These wars benefit China in many ways. Since it previously built up its energy reserves the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz does not threaten it. China already gets Turkmen and Russian energy at a discount. Iran’s dependence has grown while Washington’s military-political-economic capabilities and strategy have failed. Meanwhile Russia’s economy gains a reprieve, and a distracted Washington is increasingly unable to support Taiwan or other Asian allies as needed. Trump has proven himself to be strategically incompetent, giving China more freedom to threaten Taiwan, the Philippines, Japan, etc. In Ukraine, the lack of aid to Kyiv and energy windfalls for Russia thanks to Iran divert Western attention from Asia while Russian dependence on China grows. Lastly the war has enabled China to project air and naval power into the Middle East at an unprecedented scale.
Examine the impact of the Strait of Hormuz imbroglio on China-U.S. competition in the Middle East.
The stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz benefits China by showing what can only be described as Trump’s egregious strategic malpractice. When his ravings and utter lack of strategic capability are juxtaposed – or more precisely contraposed – to China’s steadiness, refusal to commit its military but substantial support for Iran and Russia’s war in Ukraine, Beijing looks better and better. Moreover, it diverts Washington, which has done little or nothing to push back on Chinese encroachments against Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines, or against Russia since the May summit in Beijing.
Assess the effectiveness of U.S. leadership vis-à-vis China-Russia cooperation in advancing U.S. interests in the Iran war. 
As I noted above, egregious strategic malpractice and incompetence have characterized Trump’s wartime policies, and arguably almost all of his foreign and defense policies. This war had no strategic planning, its goals change daily, and enormously damaged U.S. interests. Indeed, as of today Iran has arguably won, which benefits Russia and China. 
While the Moscow-Beijing axis is tightening in economics, politics, and military affairs; every U.S. alliance system – NATO, our alliances in Asia and in the Middle East – is under pressure or in growing disarray. Although there are some structural causes for this trend, the common denominator is Trump and his team, many of whom are equally strategically incompetent, for their attacks on allies, reckless ignorance of strategic realities, and failure to plan for this war.
Consequently, there is diminished pressure on Russia; indeed there are secret talks with it rather than support for Ukraine, China advances on our Asian allies while the administration is either silent or spouts platitudes as Assistant Secretary Colby’s tour of Southeast Asia and speech there show.  There is apparently no effort to strengthen our alliances against this Moscow-Beijing axis or the larger axis including Iran and North Korea, i.e. the CRINK. Instead, leading members of this administration regularly depreciate, devalue, or even threaten our allies, giving them reasons for distrusting America’s commitment. 
So, while our alliances are all faltering Russo-Chinese ties, along with ties among the CRINK, e.g. Iran-North Korean ties, are expanding. The contrast with the Trump administration policy is both telling and ominous.

articles.title: In Taiwan, a Disaster Exercise Prepares for Conflict, Too
articles.full_text:
This year’s natural disaster drill sought to stress-test Taiwan against cascading, multisystem failures – with obvious implications for an invasion scenario as well as an earthquake.
Polish State Fire Service and Taiwan’s Urban Search and Rescue Team conduct building collapse drill at multi-disaster training facility in Taitung, Taiwan.
In the seaside town of Taitung, four hours from Taipei by train, Taiwan’s premier national disaster preparedness exercise simulated a response to a 7.3 magnitude earthquake – layered with variables Taiwan could face in a conflict contingency. This year’s drill marked a critical operational shift, moving past standard disaster response to stress-test Taiwan against cascading, multisystem failures alongside expanded participation from regional and international partners. 
The base scenario estimated damage to 43 bridges and nearly 1,800 buildings, along with 63 casualties. Search-and-rescue teams and fire departments from seven cities and counties in Taiwan conducted a full-scale mobilization southward, while everyone on Taiwan’s cellular network received mobile alerts testing the national alert system. What was once a routine annual drill has evolved into a vital benchmark for Taiwan’s ability to manage crises requiring a whole-of-society response and international assistance.
Since 2018, the “921” exercise has commemorated the devastating September 21, 1999, Chi Chi earthquake, but its scale, complexity, and visibility increase each year. The evolution of the 921 exercise reflects Taiwan’s shift toward unscripted, full-scale scenarios modeled on U.S. curriculum. What used to be a photo-ready display of capabilities is now a deliberate effort to integrate civil government officials, military field medical teams, the private sector, and NGOs into a unified command system responsible for coordinating life-saving rescues, medical treatment, sheltering, and long-term recovery.
Particularly notable is the Taiwanese government’s willingness to test unfamiliar concepts and navigate uncertainties in front of an international audience. The 921 exercise integrates international teams and observers, many of whom face similar natural – and geopolitical – threats. The active international participation marks a key distinction between this drill and Taiwan’s Urban Resilience exercise held in June. During this year’s 921 exercise, 180 international participants brought gear and equipment to the island, working alongside local teams for three days, including the exercise’s first overnight, 24/7 continuous operation. 
A Japanese Disaster Medical Assistance Team (DMAT) coordinated with six Taiwanese DMATs, formed by local hospitals and supervised by the Ministry of Health and Welfare. In an adjacent tent, American and Taiwanese medical teams simulated joint field care. 
Additionally, 100 international observers traveled to each exercise site to observe the capabilities on display. Beyond Taiwan’s warm hospitality during events like this, international partners get to visualize what a civilian-supported response might look like during conflict – and how they might see themselves in it.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Interior aimed to establish and test a humanitarian assistance and disaster response (HADR) corridor during the 921 exercise, embedding regional allies directly into its civil resilience planning. Taiwan’s emergency responders practiced working together to salvage trapped vehicles from floodwaters in a riverbed and conducted field medical treatment alongside teams from Japan, the Philippines, and Turkiye. The exercise is also of great interest to Nordic partners like Finland, which sent firefighters to bring back lessons as they rebuild their own civil defense plans alongside a volatile neighbor.
Taiwan faces strong typhoons and regular earthquakes, requiring a professional and ready emergency response mechanism. Organizers have now begun to smartly layer these exercises with wartime injects – the scripted crisis events used to test responders. One drill simulated rescuing a downed foreign fighter pilot from the mountains, transporting him to a multinational field hospital, and then airlifting him to a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel. I watched on a livestream, powered by mobile communication units, as a stretcher was lowered onto the ship off the coast.
Each September, the 921 exercise grows in scale and complexity as responsibility rotates among cities and counties. Familiarizing jurisdictions with this integration is essential preparation. Taiwan sits between two tectonic plates, the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate, and the train from Taipei to Taitung runs through the East Rift Valley. Taitung could easily be isolated in an extreme disaster caused by an earthquake, so it’s important to test local capability. 
Beyond the natural disaster threat, China conducts continuous drills along the coastlines of Yilan County, where 921 took place in 2025, and Taitung County in the southeast. Equally serious for Taiwan’s preparation is practicing the mobilization of its resources and testing the HADR corridor with these potential, aggressive operations in mind. 
Taiwan’s government also wants to be ready to assist its neighbors, as reinforced in President Lai Ching-te’s remarks closing the exercise.

Beyond Taiwan’s warm hospitality during events like this, international partners get to visualize what a civilian-supported response might look like during conflict – and how they might see themselves in it.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Interior aimed to establish and test a humanitarian assistance and disaster response (HADR) corridor during the 921 exercise, embedding regional allies directly into its civil resilience planning. Taiwan’s emergency responders practiced working together to salvage trapped vehicles from floodwaters in a riverbed and conducted field medical treatment alongside teams from Japan, the Philippines, and Turkiye. The exercise is also of great interest to Nordic partners like Finland, which sent firefighters to bring back lessons as they rebuild their own civil defense plans alongside a volatile neighbor.
Taiwan faces strong typhoons and regular earthquakes, requiring a professional and ready emergency response mechanism. Organizers have now begun to smartly layer these exercises with wartime injects – the scripted crisis events used to test responders. One drill simulated rescuing a downed foreign fighter pilot from the mountains, transporting him to a multinational field hospital, and then airlifting him to a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel. I watched on a livestream, powered by mobile communication units, as a stretcher was lowered onto the ship off the coast.
Each September, the 921 exercise grows in scale and complexity as responsibility rotates among cities and counties. Familiarizing jurisdictions with this integration is essential preparation. Taiwan sits between two tectonic plates, the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate, and the train from Taipei to Taitung runs through the East Rift Valley. Taitung could easily be isolated in an extreme disaster caused by an earthquake, so it’s important to test local capability. 
Beyond the natural disaster threat, China conducts continuous drills along the coastlines of Yilan County, where 921 took place in 2025, and Taitung County in the southeast. Equally serious for Taiwan’s preparation is practicing the mobilization of its resources and testing the HADR corridor with these potential, aggressive operations in mind. 
Taiwan’s government also wants to be ready to assist its neighbors, as reinforced in President Lai Ching-te’s remarks closing the exercise.
In the seaside town of Taitung, four hours from Taipei by train, Taiwan’s premier national disaster preparedness exercise simulated a response to a 7.3 magnitude earthquake – layered with variables Taiwan could face in a conflict contingency. This year’s drill marked a critical operational shift, moving past standard disaster response to stress-test Taiwan against cascading, multisystem failures alongside expanded participation from regional and international partners. 
Katie Sizemore is an International Affairs Fellow in National Security, sponsored by Janine and J. Tomilson Hill, at the Council on Foreign Relations.
articles.summary: This year’s natural disaster drill sought to stress-test Taiwan against cascading, multisystem failures – with obvious implications for an invasion scenario as well as an earthquake.

articles.title: Warming Himalayas: Nepal’s Climate Justice Test
articles.full_text:
Nepal’s devastating Himalayan floods have exposed the human and economic cost of a warming region, reviving demand for climate justice.
The recent floods in Nepal exposed the growing vulnerability of Himalayan communities and the widening gap between the scale of climate losses and international support. The devastating Himalayan disaster of August 26, 2026, has left Nepal facing enormous reconstruction costs. The critical question for the global community is whether climate finance will be treated as a matter of justice, instead of charity.
The high-altitude glacier collapse in the northern part of Langtang/Lirung Mountain caused a Himalayan tsunami that killed more than 1,451 people as of September 19, 2026, left 5,786 missing, and affected about 1.6 million people in five districts of Nepal, according to the government’s situation report. 
The Nepali government has rescued 13,784 people and mobilized security forces for rescue operations. It assessed damage to 41 motorable bridges, 3,702 private houses, roads, and 12 hydropower projects.
The recently released Rapid Damage and Need Assessment (RDNA) estimates total damage and losses at more than $2.66 billion. About $4.72 billion is required for reconstruction and rehabilitation, while $5.7 million is needed for immediate relief and short-term rehabilitation over the next six months.
The flood damaged 7,570 private houses, 48 public buildings, 18 schools, seven health facilities, and 30 cultural heritage sites. About $685 million will be required to rehabilitate the social sector.
But the cost of physical damage does not capture the full social impact. Children, women, and senior citizens have suffered severe psychosocial impact, while marginalized communities have become further marginalized. These “costs” have been undermined or overlooked in the assessment report.
Scientists working with World Weather Attribution (WWA) described the disaster as a “catastrophic rock-ice avalanche that transitioned into a debris flood in the Himalayas along the Nepal-China border.” They said climate change and rising temperatures in the Himalayan region contributed significantly to the disaster. Floods in the Himalayan region have become more frequent and more devastating in recent years.
The government of Nepal has written to the Loss and Damage Fund, seeking reparation for the impacts of climate change and calling on polluters to provide compensation and justice. The Loss and Damage Fund said Nepal should provide sufficient evidence about the causes of the flood. Its board will consider providing up to $20 million in compensation. Compared with the estimated losses, the proposed support is small. 
The World Bank has also offered concessional loans to Nepal. Members of the civil society and youth are demanding grants as reparation rather than loans. They have been demanding climate justice, focusing on the causes of glacier melt in the Himalayas, known as the “Third Pole” and a source of water for large numbers of people in the region. 
Campaigners argue that the climate crisis is a fundamental human rights issue linked to the right to life and a sustainable environment. They are also calling for climate finance to be treated as justice rather than charity and for a regional framework across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region to share information, establish early-warning systems and develop institutional mechanisms.
Ten young people began a hunger strike on September 18, 2026, at the base camp of Mount Manaslu. They are demanding assessments of future glacial lake outburst flood risks, regular joint monitoring of lakes along the China-Nepal border, and climate compensation and justice for Nepal, which has to bear the costs of climate-related impacts to which it has not contributed.
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah is attending the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, where he will raise the issue of climate crisis impacting Nepal. It is an opportunity for Nepal to present the context and causes of the recent disaster internationally. Foreign Minister Sisir Khanal has already left for the UNGA and is due to attend side events in New York. He is also expected to appeal for international support to overcome the crisis.
Civil society and the public have raised concerns about delays in rescuing people trapped in a hydropower tunnel, saying the government did not allow international experts to assist during the early phase of the rescue. They have also raised concerns about delays in search operations.
Nepal will need to amplify its demands for climate justice, including through the Loss and Damage Fund, while ensuring accountability and transparency in the use of funds. The federal government’s initial hesitation to collaborate with local governments also created tensions between federal and provincial governments.
The internally displaced are being housed in 27 holding centers in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, where 1,743 people are living. The government has offered $98 (15,000 Nepali rupees) per family member to stay outside the holding centers for four months.
The disaster gives Nepal an opportunity to raise concerns about climate change at the global and regional levels. Communities living in river basins and near glacier lakes remain at high risk. Nepal should seek timely information-sharing from the international community to reduce those risks, while international partners can provide technology for faster warnings.
Existing early-warning technology and knowledge may not be sufficient to predict disasters of this kind. Investment is, therefore, needed not only for recovery but also for research and knowledge exchange. Digital technology and empowered communities could help reduce vulnerabilities.
Nepal also needs people-centered development to cope with such disasters, including the exchange of knowledge on infrastructure capable of withstanding harsh Himalayan conditions. Nepal, China, and India need to minimize human activities that directly or indirectly affect the ecology and environment of the Himalayas.
Community-led initiatives, respect for indigenous knowledge and participation in development could help sustain the region’s ecology and reduce degradation.
Small states such as Nepal need global support to rebuild after large-scale disasters. The Government of Nepal also needs to prioritize community rebuilding in future interventions rather than focusing on the business community.

articles.title: Why Is the US Eyeing Gwadar Port?
articles.full_text:
Will Washington translate its interest in Gwadar and the region around it into a policy to establish its presence there?
Berths and cranes at Gwadar Port in Pakistan’s Balochistan province.
In May, Gwadar Port handled a 53,277-ton steel billet shipment aboard a Chinese vessel whose original destination was Sohar Port in Oman. The ship was diverted to Gwadar and the Pakistani port benefited. Since the start of the U.S. war on Iran in February, Gwadar Port has welcomed several such diverted transshipments.
Over the last decade, Gwadar has struggled to attract business and maintain its economic viability on the global stage. Despite funding from China for its construction, development and connectivity as part of the larger China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), it is only in recent months that Gwadar is attracting business and seeing increased activity.  The U.S. war in Iran and the uncertainty in the Strait of Hormuz has brought in business to Gwadar that otherwise may have gone to other ports in the region.
Discussions about Gwadar Port’s potential often focus on the economic benefits to be reaped. However, it is Gwadar’s strategic location and relevance, which cannot be measured solely through the volume of cargo it handles, that makes it a prize attracting several countries.
Gwadar is situated just outside the Strait of Hormuz and across the Arabian Peninsula. Its location has been historically important from a security, trade, and geopolitical perspective.
The Iran-U.S. war has dealt a severe blow to security in the region, increased maritime trade disruptions, and thrown up geopolitical challenges. For Gwadar, the war has brought more business and, importantly, made it the focus of interest of near and distant countries. One country whose interest in Gwadar has grown since the Israel-U.S. attacks on Iran started is the United States
Washington recognized Gwadar’s importance long before Beijing’s investment in the port and CPEC began. It was, in fact, the U.S. Geological Survey of Balochistan that identified Gwadar in 1954 as a suitable location for the development of a seaport. At the time, even though it was undeveloped and small, Gwadar was already an active seaport along the Arabian Sea and was part of the maritime trade networks of the region. It was an Omani enclave until 1958, and was later transferred to Pakistan.
The United States has long considered the maritime routes in the Gulf and surrounding waters as among the most strategically important in the world, particularly because of their role in global energy supplies and shipping.
Therefore, the U.S. has maintained its presence in the waters near the Strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Peninsula since the 1940s. The U.S. Navy first established a regular presence in West Asia through the creation of the U.S. Navy Middle East Force (MEF) in 1949. Since then, the U.S. has established its naval presence throughout the region.
One of the closest such arrangements to Gwadar is in Oman. In 2019, the United States and Oman signed a deal in which Oman allowed the U.S. Navy to use the ports of Duqm and Salalah.
Hence, Gwadar’s proximity to the Strait of Hormuz, Iran, and the wider networks of strategically important maritime routes have made it very relevant to Washington’s regional interests.
This importance increased when China’s interest in the region began to grow. China’s investments in Gwadar over the years, its development of CPEC, and its maritime ambitions for Gwadar, as well as Pakistan’s close relationship with both Iran and China, added another layer to Gwadar’s importance in Washington’s eyes.
Hence, the U.S. always kept an eye on Gwadar. Now, as Gwadar’s importance surges amid the rapidly changing geopolitics in the region, it is occupying a central place on Washington’s radar.
A report from the U.S. Naval War College also identified Gwadar as a potential candidate for expanded Chinese naval operations. The report cited Pakistan’s close political, military, and economic ties with China as factors raising future possibilities for the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) at Gwadar Port.
Meanwhile, in an effort to balance its relations with China and the U.S., and amid Washington’s growing interest in Gwadar, Pakistan in September 2025 offered Washington its Pasni port, located just 100 kilometers from Gwadar.
There are also reports that, as part of the U.S. ambition to expand its maritime influence in the region and in response to concerns over China’s growing control of global port infrastructure, the Trump administration is seeking to weaken China’s influence. The U.S. plans to do so by bringing strategically important ports controlled by China under Western influence. Although the report mentioned 23 such ports, it did not identify all of them.
At the same time, the Sino-U.S. relationship is also evolving. On the one hand, relations seem to be stabilizing, even improving. Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the U.S. and his meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump hold out the possibility of cooperation between the two nations. However, this diplomatic engagement does not eliminate competition between the two big powers.
For Washington, China’s long-term and uninterrupted interest and investment in Gwadar Port and CPEC is of concern, particularly because it fears that China plans to develop strategic and military interests in the region. It has often accused China of attempting to use foreign ports owned by Chinese companies, such as Gwadar, to project naval power.
As for China, although it has not yet benefited economically from Gwadar Port, it does not want to let go of Gwadar. This is because Gwadar Port and CPEC ease China’s “Malacca Dilemma.”
While it is clear now that Gwadar’s geographic and geopolitical value far exceeds its economic benefits, whether Washington will translate its interest in Gwadar and the region around it into a policy toward establishing a presence around Gwadar remains unclear. Whether it has accepted Pakistan’s proposal for Pasni Port’s development has not been made public yet.
In May, Gwadar Port handled a 53,277-ton steel billet shipment aboard a Chinese vessel whose original destination was Sohar Port in Oman. articles.title: ASEAN: From ‘Circumvention Export Hub’ to ‘Value Creation Hub’
articles.full_text:
As the U.S.-China rivalry hollows out the WTO, Japan and ASEAN have a chance to build something new.
The huge Chinese market and its BRI infrastructure investments remain highly attractive to ASEAN, China’s recession notwithstanding. Chinese manufacturing investment is also expanding, reinforcing ASEAN’s position as a key part of global production hubs and supply chains.
This growth model carries inherent risks, however. Dependence on China for key components and intermediate goods is raising American suspicions that ASEAN may be a hub for Chinese goods being rerouted to third-country markets. Beyond that, if the model hardens into simple assembly of Chinese-origin inputs for export to third countries, it will limit the added value and economic impact generated within the region itself.
At the same time, long seen as a counterweight to China, the United States is no longer an unconditionally reliable partner. While maintaining security engagement, Washington has distanced itself from the GATT and WTO free trade order that underpinned ASEAN’s growth, showing little inclination to open its own markets while imposing unilateral high tariffs in the name of reciprocity.
Yet ASEAN’s challenge is not merely a choice between the United States and China. It faces a new dilemma: deeper production dependence on China will stoke American wariness, while abruptly severing that dependence would damage the region’s own industrial base. What is needed is a framework that avoids over-reliance on either side, lets ASEAN generate its own value, and preserves the region’s freedom to choose its markets and partners.
This is where new opportunities for “co-creation” between Japan and ASEAN emerge. Going beyond conventional support for industrialization, the aim is to advance ASEAN jointly into a production region that generates distinctive value for global markets, based on industrial clusters and supply chains formed through investment by Japanese companies over many years.
First, ASEAN should shift from conventional assembly and export to become a high value-added “value creation hub” covering everything from research and development to design, components and materials, production, certification, and services. The key is not to exclude China. While continuing to source components from China and elsewhere, the idea is to promote substantial processing and accumulation of technology and knowledge within ASEAN itself, generating employment and income in the process. Call this “Made in ASEAN 2.0.” The label signals to global markets that these are not Chinese goods merely rerouted through ASEAN, but products whose value was created in ASEAN.
Second, the priority is to apply the expertise Japanese companies have accumulated in human resource development, local supplier formation, production management, and technology transfer to next-generation industries such as EVs, semiconductors, digital solutions, AI, green transformation, and critical minerals. Japanese companies will also need to pivot from “making in ASEAN” to investing in “creating value in ASEAN,” including through research, development, and design.
Third, ASEAN itself needs to further deepen AFTA (ASEAN Free Trade Area), harmonize non-tariff measures, standards, certifications, and customs systems, and push the eleven markets toward a more unified production and market space. The ASEAN Geoeconomics Report 2025 proposed a common external tariff (CET) as an old idea worth bringing back. A CET can support intra-regional procurement of parts and materials and the formation of regional supply chains. Japan should link institutional integration with corporate investment and technology transfer, to help build “Made in ASEAN 2.0” together with ASEAN.
Rebuilding free trade from Japan and ASEAN
Industrial policy alone cannot deliver “Made in ASEAN 2.0.” As the free trade system erodes between the United States and China, Japan and ASEAN should take on the task of rebuilding the rules for the next era.
With Japan and ASEAN at the center, existing FTA and EPA networks — CPTPP, RCEP, AFTA, and the Japan-EU EPA — can serve to connect middle powers such as the EU, Canada, Australia, South Korea, and India. All are ASEAN dialogue partners, and existing ministerial and summit meetings provide ready forums. The first step is to promote institutional connectivity where cooperation is already feasible: rules of origin, digital trade, customs clearance, certifications, green products, and supply chain transparency.
This is not a “third bloc” designed to challenge the United States and China. It is an open network that complements the WTO, available to any country or region willing to accept transparent rules, without closing the door on Washington or Beijing. The goal is not a new bloc but the overcoming of polarization itself.
What Japan should offer ASEAN is more options — connections to multiple markets, technologies, capital, and supply networks.
The common goal of Japan and ASEAN should not be simply free trade that lowers tariffs. It should be next-generation free trade in which where value is created is clearly identifiable, and that value flows back to production regions as employment, technology, and income. ASEAN would be transformed from a hub for rerouted exports into a value creation hub, a model that could be extended to other middle powers. This is the “third path” to overcoming U.S.-China polarization.
