articles.title: Trump and Xi: Strongmen at the Temple of Thymos
articles.full_text:
The ego-driven fragility of a world run by recognition-hungry autocrats.
U.S. President Donald Trump tours the Temple of Heaven in Beijing with China’s President Xi Jinping, May 14, 2026.
I want to propose a lens for power rivalry that’s equally ancient but different and complementary: a Thymos Trap. 
This desire for status, as the journalist Will Storr explained in “The Status Game,” is pursued through dominance, virtue, or success. These differing tactics can depend on the cultures in which status-seeking individuals operate. 
According to political philosopher Ye Xue, in the United States, where status is relative and must be defended, the cultural tendency is to pursue self-esteem through demands for honor. China, by contrast, is rooted in a stable hierarchy in which status is relational and harmony is sought. Trump and Xi represent these different cultural approaches to recognition perfectly; Trump’s is deeply individualistic and even antagonistic, while Xi’s is more concerned with a collective megalothymia that demands deference to China as a whole.
For all their differences, Xi and Trump share a common insistence on staking their own legitimacy on the nation’s self-esteem, updating French King Louis XIV’s apocryphal line, l’État, c’est moi (“I am the State”). But they do differ in noteworthy ways. Per Ye Xue’s research, Trump demands conspicuous displays of deference to him as an individual, while Xi is more concerned with displays of “face” – something he has fused with gestures toward China as a whole. In that way, Xi is a quintessentially Chinese statesman, in being tactful, understated, and formal.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney reflected after a January 2026 meeting with Xi how the general secretary had said something to him to the effect of “don’t lecture me in public.” Xi wasn’t averse to hearing complaints, Carney implied, but to be seen being criticized was an unacceptable loss of face. 
The U.S. president, meanwhile, has a grammar that is distinctly American. The historian Walter Russell Mead identified Trump as following in the line of President Andrew Jackson’s heirs: populist, informal, and quick to respond to insults. Trump must win visibly while Xi must not lose face. They are reflective of their different cultural traditions but are variations on the same substance. And they suffer from the same paradox of outward strength and inward fragility.
Internationally, it’s equally fragile, because when a regime stakes its legitimacy on delivering ever-more recognition to a lone individual, then foreign humiliation becomes a domestic survival threat. The insistence on recognition is not a personality footnote but essential to national identity, requiring displays of deference. In “The Red Emperor,” Michael Sheridan related an anecdote from 2011: Xi told a visiting U.S. Vice President Joe Biden the lesson he’d drawn from history was that China must never make concessions. But compromises, power-sharing, and diffused power centers are inherent to the nature of the modern state system, which means such perceived humiliations are inevitable.
A trend like the Thymos Trap operates over the long term, and some caveats should be acknowledged. The serious disarray in what used to be called the Western alliance means that autocratic systems in China and Russia look more harmonious and even attractive to some doomsayers than liberal democracies. After the meeting in May between Xi and Trump, the headline on a Hal Brands column lamented that “Xi sets the terms for everyone now.” 
The Communist Party leader radiates the confidence and gravitas of a man who appears to have mastered his thymos. But the Thymos Trap ensnares leaders because the fragility it engenders is structural, not peculiar to their individual pathology. Their regimes have the same architectural drawbacks, regardless of their national flavors. The same impulses that propel a one-man cult become the forces that bedevil it. The trap is that strongmen must keep appearing strong – and whether their opiate of choice is honor or face, the performance eventually consumes the substance. The counter-model to the thymos-doomed leader would be Marcus Aurelius, the Roman Emperor who interrogated his own status-hunger by wielding near-absolute power with a brake on it in the form of Stoicism. Xi styles himself as this sort of contemplative, omnipotent philosopher-king, and yet his heavily propagandized “Xi Jinping Thought” is most likely the ghost-written output of a CCP committee. Marcus is the inversion, the vanishingly rare leader who distrusts and even resists his own urges for recognition, challenging his own thymos in a private notebook. Leaders like that are few and far between, a tragic reality that only highlights the ever-present danger of the Thymos Trap.
I want to propose a lens for power rivalry that’s equally ancient but different and complementary: a Thymos Trap. 
This desire for status, as the journalist Will Storr explained in “The Status Game,” is pursued through dominance, virtue, or success. These differing tactics can depend on the cultures in which status-seeking individuals operate. 
According to political philosopher Ye Xue, in the United States, where status is relative and must be defended, the cultural tendency is to pursue self-esteem through demands for honor. China, by contrast, is rooted in a stable hierarchy in which status is relational and harmony is sought. Trump and Xi represent these different cultural approaches to recognition perfectly; Trump’s is deeply individualistic and even antagonistic, while Xi’s is more concerned with a collective megalothymia that demands deference to China as a whole.
For all their differences, Xi and Trump share a common insistence on staking their own legitimacy on the nation’s self-esteem, updating French King Louis XIV’s apocryphal line, l’État, c’est moi (“I am the State”). But they do differ in noteworthy ways. Per Ye Xue’s research, Trump demands conspicuous displays of deference to him as an individual, while Xi is more concerned with displays of “face” – something he has fused with gestures toward China as a whole. In that way, Xi is a quintessentially Chinese statesman, in being tactful, understated, and formal.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney reflected after a January 2026 meeting with Xi how the general secretary had said something to him to the effect of “don’t lecture me in public.” Xi wasn’t averse to hearing complaints, Carney implied, but to be seen being criticized was an unacceptable loss of face. 
The U.S. president, meanwhile, has a grammar that is distinctly American. The historian Walter Russell Mead identified Trump as following in the line of President Andrew Jackson’s heirs: populist, informal, and quick to respond to insults. Trump must win visibly while Xi must not lose face. They are reflective of their different cultural traditions but are variations on the same substance. And they suffer from the same paradox of outward strength and inward fragility.
Internationally, it’s equally fragile, because when a regime stakes its legitimacy on delivering ever-more recognition to a lone individual, then foreign humiliation becomes a domestic survival threat. The insistence on recognition is not a personality footnote but essential to national identity, requiring displays of deference. In “The Red Emperor,” Michael Sheridan related an anecdote from 2011: Xi told a visiting U.S. Vice President Joe Biden the lesson he’d drawn from history was that China must never make concessions. But compromises, power-sharing, and diffused power centers are inherent to the nature of the modern state system, which means such perceived humiliations are inevitable.
A trend like the Thymos Trap operates over the long term, and some caveats should be acknowledged. The serious disarray in what used to be called the Western alliance means that autocratic systems in China and Russia look more harmonious and even attractive to some doomsayers than liberal democracies. After the meeting in May between Xi and Trump, the headline on a Hal Brands column lamented that “Xi sets the terms for everyone now.” 
The Communist Party leader radiates the confidence and gravitas of a man who appears to have mastered his thymos. But the Thymos Trap ensnares leaders because the fragility it engenders is structural, not peculiar to their individual pathology. Their regimes have the same architectural drawbacks, regardless of their national flavors. The same impulses that propel a one-man cult become the forces that bedevil it. The trap is that strongmen must keep appearing strong – and whether their opiate of choice is honor or face, the performance eventually consumes the substance. Leaders like that are few and far between, a tragic reality that only highlights the ever-present danger of the Thymos Trap.
When U.S. President Donald Trump made his second state visit to China in May 2026, Xi Jinping escorted him through Beijing’s magisterial Temple of Heaven, where the Ming and Qing emperors performed rites that mediated between heaven and the earthly order. But when these two men with autocratic impulses and outsized egos strolled through the complex, it became not a Temple of Heaven but a Temple of Thymos – a stage for distributing recognition rather than cosmic concerns. Now, the neoclassical architecture of the White House provides the set for their September 23–25 encounter.  Readers of The Diplomat can find in it many articles on the “Thucydides Trap” popularized by the political scientist Graham Allison. The Thucydides Trap suggests that China and the United States are headed for inevitable conflict. Several scholars dispute Allison’s reading, and yet the ancient historian’s ghost still hovered as Xi and Trump moved through the temple, with the Chinese Communist Party’s general secretary, who has a pattern of citing Allison, even referencing the phrase.
I want to propose a lens for power rivalry that’s equally ancient but different and complementary: a Thymos Trap.

articles.summary: The ego-driven fragility of a world run by recognition-hungry autocrats.

articles.title: 3 Ts Will Dominate the Trump-Xi Summit
articles.full_text:
Expect little movement on trade, less on Taiwan, and who knows on tech.
U.S. President Donald Trump bids farewell to China’s President Xi Jinping at Zhongnanhai in Beijing, China, May 15, 2026.
When Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping last sat down in May 2026, talk was centered on three Ts: trade, technology and Taiwan. Their next summit, due to begin in the United States on September 24, looks set to focus on the same set of issues again. The main difference will be that the technology element has been given added urgency by the sudden and rapid shift in developments in artificial intelligence.
What’s less clear is whether the two sides will be able to come to any sort of transformative agreement on that, or any other issue.
The most urgent issue, but also the simplest to solve, will be on trade. Nearly a year ago at Busan in South Korea, Trump and Xi hammered out an agreement whereby the United States agreed to lift some export controls on high-end technology and to reduce the then three-figure tariffs on Chinese goods. For its part, China agreed not to restrict the flow of critical minerals and rare earths to U.S. users.
That pact – only good for one year – is now up for renewal. Both sides are likely to want a continuation of the current arrangement, and while there may be some tweaking on the side, the new deal will probably be similar to the old one.
Each side has proposed in previous meetings that there should be a new instrument, a Board of Trade, that will assess non-sensitive China-U.S. business interests. However, details about the institution remains vague. Some announcements are likely during the summit, but business leaders will want to know how comprehensive and lasting the arrangements for the board will be.
There is still less information on a proposed Board of Investment, which remains on the drawing board. The Chinese side has proposed bringing major Chinese CEOs to the summit to match the likes of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk – both of whom accompanied Trump on the Beijing trip. But the choice of business leaders is likely to turn on which aspects of trade China thinks are likely to develop most effectively in the short term.
Taiwan is a much harder issue to solve, but it’s unlikely that much that is discussed on Xi’s visit will determine its outcome.
Trump has been less willing than his predecessor to commit the United States to defending the island should Beijing invade, instead reasserting Washington’s long-held position of strategic ambiguity.
And although the U.S. is currently distracted from East Asia by the Iran conflict, China still prefers to find methods short of war to bring the island under Beijing’s control.
The island’s January 2028 presidential election is likely to be a more crucial moment for Taiwan’s future, particularly if the opposition – and more China-friendly – Kuomintang (KMT) wins the presidency, or indeed if an isolationist candidate becomes U.S. president later that year. If the next U.S. president opted to change course by taking a less active involvement in overseas issues – as has been floated by early contenders on both the left and right – that would change things all the more.
For now, Beijing will continue to build the People’s Liberation Army’s naval capacity to have the option of military action against the island. But its preference will be to take advantage of changes within Taiwan’s internal politics while combining economic incentives and coercion, squeezing Taipei’s international footprint and hoping for a slackening of U.S. interest in the western Pacific.
Other international issues are likely to gain less attention. China is expected to make clear its unhappiness about the war on Iran, and the U.S. may remind China that it has passed new legislation allowing sanctions on countries that buy Russian oil – of which, China is the largest purchaser. However, neither issue is likely to lead to any major change in practice.
It’s really in the area of tech, and AI in particular, where both sides will be trying to make diplomacy catch up with reality. The May summit surprised many because the question of mutual agreement on regulation of AI came up in a way that had not been on the agenda for the first year of the Trump administration.
However, both sides agreed that talks in principle about regulation might be possible and even desirable because of the growth in the importance, but also unpredictability, of AI. And on September 20, the United States and China mooted the idea of a “hotline” to notify the other over AI national security risks.
Between the May and September summits, fears about AI in the U.S have created an increasingly unfriendly atmosphere toward unregulated AI.
In China, public sentiment about AI is less openly hostile and some of its major benefits in areas such as health care have softened people’s attitudes. Yet there are still plenty of concerns expressed in private about whether China’s troubled economy will definitively benefit from the AI boom. Although many argue it has created new opportunities for consumers, others point to the relatively few jobs that have been created for a workforce that finds itself buffeted by wide-scale job elimination.
Both the U.S. and China have reasons to talk about AI regulation. The alarming prospect of rogue AI companies causing intense social disruptions through their business choices is clearly one such reason, and in the U.S., voters’ more immediate concerns about data centers are another.
There are also China-specific reasons that Beijing may seek restraint. One of the most common concerns about AI is that it may well run out of control. And “out of control” is a kryptonite phrase for the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party. That’s particularly true of Xi who, as a youth, spent years in rural exile after his father fell to a purge just before the Cultural Revolution – an upheaval during which China’s politics turned to anarchy. It was a formative experience for Xi, which has no doubt influenced his tendencies as a leader toward exercising as much control as possible.
AI that undermines the unchallengeable leadership of the Communist Party would be an unwelcome guest in China’s cyberspace, and regulation that solves that problem would not be rejected out of hand.
However, this recognition of mutual concern about AI – albeit for very different reasons – is still not likely to see much progress in the short term. The competition between the U.S. and China on AI is real, and neither governments nor private sector actors in either country are willing to make concessions that could advantage the other side.
Levels of trust between Washington and Beijing remain very low on the issue. Talks about talks seem the most likely public outcome, though what happens behind the scenes may be pursued more discreetly.
The Trump-Xi summit is less important in terms of any major change in policy on either side, and more because it marks part of a commitment to maintain some form of dialogue between the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries. The leaders may well meet twice more in the near future, at the APEC and G20 summits, to be hosted by China and the United States, respectively.
To meet four times in just over half a year is a good sign; refusal to meet would be much more worrying. But the underlying difficulties of the three Ts, where the leaders seem to have fundamentally incompatible agendas, remain the thread beneath the ostensibly polite and occasionally amiable conversations.

articles.title: A Debate Is Raging in China Over English Education
articles.full_text:
Rising youth unemployment, the advent of AI translation, and growing anger against everything foreign are fueling public anger against English education in China.
In the heated public discussions in China over English education, those calling to downgrade or abandon English in Chinese schools and colleges are using an ancient saying: 刻舟求剑 (ke zhou qiu jian), literally “notching the boat to find a sword.” Less literally, the phrase describes a foolish approach to solving problems that fails to account for changing circumstances.
The phrase refers to an ancient fable from the Warring States period (475 BC to 221 BC). In the story, a traveler from the State of Chu was crossing a river in a boat when his precious sword accidentally slipped from his hand and fell into the water. Instead of diving into the water to retrieve it, he calmly took out a small knife and carved a notch on the side of the boat right where the sword fell. 
On being asked why he didn’t immediately jump into the river to retrieve his sword, he replied: “There is no need to worry. My sword fell into the river at this marked place. As soon as the boat reaches the dock and pulls into shore, I will jump down from here to retrieve my sword.” 
That’s the context needed to understand those using this idiom in order to ridicule the continuation of English being taught in primary, secondary and high schools. Critics point out that the decision to incorporate the English language as a mandatory part of the school curriculum was made 50 years ago. “At the time, the aim was to quickly strengthen education, learn science and technology from abroad, and improve the overall quality of the population. Forcing everyone to learn English, while perhaps a bit of an overreaction, was understandable given the specific circumstances,” Chinese scholar Xiang Ligang commented on WeChat. But, like the position of the boat in the fable, China’s circumstances have changed.  
It’s a widely held figure that English learning for a Chinese student – from early schooling to entering a university, in total 12 years of education – requires 3,000 to 5,000 hours of study and at least 100,000 yuan. Many in China are raising the question: is it worth it?
Arguments against the continuation of English as a compulsory subject in schools and colleges were recently further strengthened by a call to “end English’s core status” issued by Tang Jiafeng. Tang is a mathematics professor and online celebrity who has long taught mathematics to candidates taking postgraduate entrance examinations. The latest controversy stemmed from his comments on reforms to the locally administered zhongkao (senior high school entrance examination). Saying that “the history of Chinese people worshiping foreign things and fawning on foreign countries should end,” he advocated for reducing the weight given to English proficiency on the exam.  
Currently, English is a required subject starting in third grade. It is weighted on par with Chinese language and mathematics on the entrance exam for secondary schools, the central exam after ninth grade, and the high school graduation exam. Chinese, English, and mathematics (collectively known as CEM) are the three most important subjects on the gaokao, China’s college and university entrance examination. Each subject counts for 150 points out of a total of 750.   
Tang Jiafeng called for downgrading the status of English as part of an angry reaction to Chinese history being removed as a scoring subject in exams in several provinces. A large section of China’s nationalist intellectuals – who are also generally labeled as “conservatives” – have come out in support of Tang. Also on their side are parents and students who oppose making English a compulsory subject. English is considered difficult in China, since the Chinese language does not use an alphabetic script. Learning English thus increases the students’ burden and parents’ or guardian’s financial pressure. 
Many also ask whether there’s any point to the effort. Given the difficulty involved in mastering a language with an entirely different writing system, rote memorization without real understanding is common. Xiang, in the WeChat commentary cited above, claimed that “95 percent of people who have studied English in primary [school], secondary [school], and university cannot communicate fluently, and 90 percent of those who have studied English will never use it in their lives, except for exams. Learning English without mastering it is a widespread phenomenon.” This argument has gained weight with the advent of AI-enabled translation. 
A number of intellectuals, joined by several influential leftist scholars in leading universities, have thus challenged the status of English as a compulsory subject. Other well-known public figures – such as the former Global Times editor Hu Xijin – are defending the primacy of Chinese, English, and mathematics. 
Hu in particular rubbished Tang’s claim that English learning was a sign of foreign-worship, saying “only an extreme and narrow-minded group regarded learning English as xenocentric.” Upholding English as the key for modernization and global competitiveness, Hu countered Tang by claiming that English had attained its global status because the West had led modernization for several centuries. “As China rises, the usage of Chinese to describe inventions and innovations is steadily increasing, while the center of gravity in science, technology and the economy is also shifting towards Chinese. But that will be a long process…” Hu said. “Turning this issue into one charged with ‘patriotism’ will only prove counter-productive, leading to unnecessary ideological dispute and confusion.”
Nationalist and leftist scholars dismissed Hu’s argument that English is crucial for China’s science, technology and economy. They cite the example of the outstanding post-World War II industrial and commercial growth of Germany, France, Japan – all of which succeeded without widespread English fluency. 
Taking the argument further, these scholars actually blamed English classes for having stymied the growth of STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) in China in recent years. Last week, a Chinese article, in an apparent appeal to the authorities to break the “English shackles” wrote: “Using an excessively heavy burden of English learning and overly difficult English exams as an important criterion for ‘selecting talent’ has led to the elimination of many science and engineering talents who are not good at English, which has a serious negative impact on the cultivation of STEM professionals and the tackling of technological bottlenecks in my country” (emphasis added).
Liu Qing and Liu Yun, joint authors of the article, cited the specific example of Wang Xingxing, founder and CEO of Unitree Robotics, who almost didn’t test into university due to his poor English. Yet Wang currently enjoys a “rock star” status; he appeared on the cover of Time magazine two months ago with his manned mecha robot GD0, for a story entitled “The Age of Robots is Coming.” A year before that, Wang became a sensation in China after being invited to speak in the presence of Xi Jinping at the Beijing Symposium for private enterprises in February 2025. The other five speakers included Ren Zhengfei of Huawei fame, Lin Jun of Xiaomi, BYD founder Wang Chuanfu, Liu Yonghao of the New Hope Group, and Yu Renrong, popularly known as “China’s semiconductor king.”  
Wang’s weak command of English nearly ruined his emergence as what Time called “an atypical prophet of the AI era.” As Liu Qing and Liu Yun pointed out, in spite of achieving outstanding scores in science subjects, due to his poor performance on the English language portion of entrance exams, Wang was forced to go to second-tier universities in Hangzhou and Shanghai for his graduation and postgraduate degrees respectively.
Liu Qing and Liu Yun underscored the fact that many potential scientific talents like Wang are being eliminated in the college entrance examination or postgraduate entrance examination solely because of their poor English skills. They believe that Wang was lucky to avoid this fate. To all those in China who are opposing English as a core subject in schools, this has become a modern-day example of the tragedy of “dying before achieving one’s goal.” 
There are several distinct threads to the argument: nationalist (Chinese people shouldn’t be forced to learn a foreign language), utilitarian (mandatory English classes don’t actually achieve the goal of linguistic proficiency), and practical (poor English skills could prematurely end the careers of those gifted in STEM fields). articles.title: America’s AI Safety Dilemma and the Trump-Xi Summit
articles.full_text:
Washington will not slow its own AI labs. Slowing China’s instead would look like safety policy, but it could cost the United States the one AI deal within reach this week.
On September 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” arguing that the leading labs should deliberately slow how fast their models gain new capabilities. Within hours, his chief rivals lined up behind him: Sam Altman said OpenAI would match Anthropic’s commitment to host independent evaluators, and Elon Musk replied, “Dario is right.” 
Two days later, U.S. President Donald Trump called fears of an AI catastrophe a hoax and claimed that amid the backlash against AI and data centers, “the only one that is happy about it is China.” 
That exchange hangs over Xi Jinping’s arrival in Washington this week, the first state visit by a Chinese leader in more than a decade. 
The AI pacing debate is a dilemma the Trump administration cannot resolve at home. There is rising pressure from the public to slow down, but the government is convinced that slowing down means losing to China. The easiest way out runs through Beijing. If Washington will not slow American AI, it can try to slow Chinese AI instead, through tighter controls on chips, compute, and access to American models. That option is tempting precisely because it is an area where the safety-minded and the competition-focused, the labs and the White House, already agree. 
But Trump should know that choosing this path would also undercut the most promising AI outcome on the summit table.
Public calls to slow the pace of AI development are growing in urgency. In a new Politico poll, 63 percent of respondents saw a real chance that AI could wipe out humanity, and a CBS News/YouGov survey found that most Americans want AI development slowed, though not stopped. With the midterms weeks away, AI risk is becoming an electoral issue, and the labs’ own warnings have lent that anxiety new credibility.
The Trump administration has treated the debate as a threat to American primacy. Trump said he wants to stay ahead of China because “whoever wins AI wins.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that there is “no day after tomorrow if China wins” on AI – “nothing [else] would matter.” 
Politico’s polling showed that Americans are split, 43 percent to 37 percent, on whether falling behind other countries is acceptable in exchange for safer AI. However, Trump’s supporters have a clear opinion: people who voted for him in 2024 preferred staying in the AI race (50 percent) to prioritizing safety issues (38 percent).
Since Trump is unwilling to slow down AI development and risk falling behind, that leaves the administration searching for a way to look serious about AI risk without constraining American labs. Amodei had a suggestion. The Anthropic CEO’s plan recommended an “attempt to coordinate with authoritarian governments, to the extent this is possible, while taking seriously the challenges of verifying compliance.” Beijing is at the top of the list of authoritarian governments to talk with.
Even while calling for coordination, however, Amodei urged the Trump administration to keep “powerful AI chips or semiconductor manufacturing equipment” out of Chinese hands, close “chip smuggling operations” and remote access to data centers, “crack down on unauthorized distillation,” and harden labs against theft of model weights. Amodei explicitly agreed with Bessent that “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world.” In his framework, safety at home depends on a durable lead abroad. 
That points to a clear area of overlap: the White House can embrace the “slow China” half of the AI industry’s agenda while rejecting the “slow ourselves” half. This is already playing out.
Earlier this month, the NSA, FBI, and CISA jointly accused six Chinese developers, including DeepSeek and Alibaba, of industrial-scale distillation of American frontier models. In July Bessent said Washington could sanction firms found stealing from American models. Trump and Xi are also expected to discuss whether Chinese firms can keep renting top Nvidia compute through Southeast Asian data centers, while the suspension of the Affiliates Rule, which extends export blacklists to affiliates of listed firms, expires with the Busan truce in November.
On semiconductors, restricting Chinese access would be a bigger shift. The Trump administration has cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies to buy Nvidia’s H200 chips, though Chinese customs has kept nearly all the chips out. But a restriction package lets the White House tell anxious voters it is acting on AI risk while asking nothing of American companies. The louder the domestic debate grows, the better that trade looks.
Beijing has already read the room and decided this is the most likely outcome of the United States’ AI pacing debate. China’s Foreign Ministry answered Amodei’s essay by warning that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition” would disrupt global AI governance. The state-run Global Times called the slowdown push a “Cold War playbook” for the sector. China’s Commerce Ministry threatened “resolute countermeasures” if Washington uses the distillation accusations to suppress Chinese firms. Among other options, China could resurrect the rare earth exports controls that were suspended under the Busan truce.
Beijing’s official line is not the whole Chinese conversation, though. This spring, two of China’s most senior AI governance figures – Xue Lan, who chairs China’s national expert committee on AI governance, and Zeng Yi, dean of the Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance – joined a Capitol Hill discussion convened by Senator Bernie Sanders. Xue acknowledged the geopolitical rivalry but called for “safe zones” where American and Chinese scientists can build safety standards and protocols together. Zeng, whose institute has catalogued 94 classes of AI safety threats, warned last week that AI’s catastrophic risks, including “the hidden danger of human extinction,” are mounting daily. Both Xue and Zeng helped draft China’s national AI governance principles.
The Trump administration now has a real AI safety deliverable within reach. In New York on September 20, Bessent proposed a standing China-U.S. AI dialogue with a way for each side to flag AI incidents serious enough to threaten national security. A standing channel would be a first for Trump’s second term: the AI consultations he and Xi discussed in Beijing in May were never formalized. Beijing’s response, however, was unclear.
 U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said chip export controls were not part of the AI safety mechanism discussions. That separation is the right instinct, but Beijing is likely to see the two issues as inextricably linked. If China sees “AI safety” as a synonym for containment, voices like Xue’s and Zeng’s lose ground at home. Beijing will worry that every notification through the new channel creates a pretext for new restrictions on Chinese companies. 
China-U.S. crisis management mechanisms already have a poor record. After the United States shot down a Chinese high-altitude balloon that had traversed the U.S. mainland in February 2023, Beijing declined a call from the U.S. defense secretary, later explaining that Washington had not created “the proper atmosphere” for dialogue. An AI incident channel that China sees as an extension of the technology war will go quiet exactly when it is needed.
Amodei anticipated this objection and rejected it, arguing that restrictions “increase the leverage held by democracies and make an agreement more likely in the future.” That may hold for a treaty negotiated from a position of strength years from now, but not for an incident channel that runs on day-to-day trust. Amodei himself wrote that sharing information about misaligned models can have value even without formal agreements. That is exactly what a notification channel would do.
Washington can manage this dilemma without breaking the Trump-Xi summit. If the Trump-Xi summit needs a first substantive commitment, Amodei’s essay suggested a modest one: an agreement that neither side will use AI to produce biological weapons.
Beyond that, the leaders should establish the notification mechanism as a standalone safety channel, insulated from trade and technology-control disputes, and pair it with a technical track that brings government evaluators at the Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation together with experts like Xue and Zeng. That track could define what counts as a reportable incident and build shared tests for biological and cyber risks without touching the chips, compute, and model weights where the race is actually run. It would also serve U.S. primacy: if Bessent is right that the real threat to AI safety is “letting any nation other than the United States set the global standard,” Washington should want to be in the room when Chinese experts help write one.
To make cooperation on AI risk more feasible, the United States should call its restrictions what they are. Enforcement against model distillation or chip smuggling may be justified on intellectual property or security grounds, but selling it as the answer to AI risk lets the White House dodge the domestic aspect of AI safety while poisoning the bilateral effort. 
The domestic question needs a domestic answer. Bessent has shown an openness to safety concerns. Testifying before the House Financial Services Committee on September 15, he rejected the liability exemption the labs are seeking, arguing that safety is best guaranteed when developers are “liable for what they build and generate.” The independent evaluators that Anthropic and OpenAI have agreed to host do not require the United States to fall behind anyone. 
The pacing debate asked Washington to voluntarily slow down AI development. The administration’s answer is that China should be forced to slow down instead. That may play well at home, but it will not make American AI any safer, and it risks scuttling a China-U.S. channel on AI risk before it even begins. 
Trump insists the AI race is winner-take-all. This week he can show that staying ahead of China and talking to it about shared risks are not mutually exclusive.
On September 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” arguing that the leading labs should deliberately slow how fast their models gain new capabilities. Within hours, his chief rivals lined up behind him: Sam Altman said OpenAI would match Anthropic’s commitment to host independent evaluators, and Elon Musk replied, “Dario is right.” 
Two days later, U.S. President Donald Trump called fears of an AI catastrophe a hoax and claimed that amid the backlash against AI and data centers, “the only one that is happy about it is China.” 
That exchange hangs over Xi Jinping’s arrival in Washington this week, the first state visit by a Chinese leader in more than a decade. 
The AI pacing debate is a dilemma the Trump administration cannot resolve at home. There is rising pressure from the public to slow down, but the government is convinced that slowing down means losing to China. The easiest way out runs through Beijing. If Washington will not slow American AI, it can try to slow Chinese AI instead, through tighter controls on chips, compute, and access to American models. That option is tempting precisely because it is an area where the safety-minded and the competition-focused, the labs and the White House, already agree.
articles.summary: Washington will not slow its own AI labs. Slowing China’s instead would look like safety policy, but it could cost the United States the one AI deal within reach this week.

articles.title: SCO, BRICS, Trump-Xi: What Does the Spate of Summits Mean for India?
articles.full_text:
This year’s summit season reveals conflicting visions of global order (and India’s place in it).
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi addresses the 2026 BRICS summit as Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin listen, New Delhi, India, Sep. 13, 2026.
The world is once again in the midst of summit season. The conclusion of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan at the start of September was followed by the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India last week. This week’s United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York is likely to be overshadowed by the summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump on September 24. And before the year’s end, the APEC Summit will also take place in China in November followed by the United States hosting the G20 Summit in December. 
Each of these summits offers a different vision of the international order. The SCO and BRICS both represent the Global South, advocating for a more equitable distribution of power in a multipolar global order. But the SCO has traditionally offered a more anti-Western worldview relative to the non-Western worldview propagated by the BRICS. 
Reflecting this, the SCO’s Bishkek Declaration was more vocal in calling out the Israeli-U.S. attacks on Iran by “condemning military strikes” against the country, adding that “such actions violate the principles and norms of international law” and “create serious risks to international peace, security and stability.” In contrast, the BRICS’ New Delhi Declaration raised the Iran conflict without making specific reference to the actions of the United States in starting the conflict. It expressed “deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions” while calling for “maximum restraint” by all parties, as well as ensuring the “protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure,” “respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of states, and maintaining the “smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy.”
Meanwhile, the U.N. General Assembly is increasingly seen as an outdated forum from a bygone era when universal values, norms, and rules were bywords for the state of the international order. In contrast, the Trump-Xi meeting reflects the world we are living in now with a more power-driven, “might makes right” international system.
Each vision has its own advocates. The United States under the Trump administration clearly favors power over principle, with a preference for bilateral interactions between so-called great powers. This has been reflected in Trump’s proclivity for one-on-one meetings with strongman leaders, such as Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska last August and the meeting with Xi in Beijing in May. The Trumpian worldview also favors unilateral action as noted by the so-called Donroe Doctrine, which advocates a “spheres of influence” approach toward international relations.
Meanwhile, China seeks to project an image of itself as a more responsible power compared to the United States. In doing so, it advocates for multilateralism and upholding the rules-based international order through its support for the United Nations for example. However, in reality Beijing is increasingly leaning in the direction of unilateral action through acts of economic coercion – leveraging its centrality to global supply chains, particularly in critical and emerging technologies – and gray zone tactics, as evidenced by its actions in the Taiwan Strait and South China Sea. It also seeks to use forums that represent the Global South to propagate its own worldviews, embedded in its four initiatives: the Global Development, Governance, Security, and Civilization Initiatives. 
Where does this leave countries like India? 
New Delhi has demonstrated a fondness for hosting large summits, from its G20 Summit in 2023 to the AI Impact Summit earlier this year and now the BRICS Summit (the fourth time India has hosted the latter). In all these forums India has sought to promote itself as a so-called voice of the Global South. As G20 president, India facilitated the entry of the African Union into the grouping. At the AI Impact Summit, it advocated for the “democratization” of artificial intelligence (echoing its rhetoric on digital inclusion through promoting Digital Public Infrastructure). 
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s speech at the 2026 BRICS Summit continued this narrative by calling for transforming the Global South “from rule takers into rule-shapers.” He described the current structure of global governance as a “pyramid of privilege,” with the Global South being on the “front row of global crises, but the backrow of decision-making.” 
Modi’s remarks could be seen as a counterpart to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s speech at the Davos World Economic Forum earlier this year. But whereas Carney’s remarks were seen as a “call to arms” for the world’s middle powers, Modi’s were marching orders for the Global South.
As chair of this year’s BRICS Summit, New Delhi also sought to promote a more benign and inclusive worldview, adopting the slogan of “Humanity First,” which was complemented by Modi’s “people-centric” approach. In doing so, however, India’s worldview appears out of sync with the current state of the world order, which is increasingly fragmented and plagued by multiple conflicts. 
This comes at a time when forums like BRICS are being squeezed by newer groupings. On one side are bilateral summits between major powers such as this week’s Trump-Xi meeting. As the world’s technology superpowers, it is more likely that China and the United States will set the terms on AI regulation at their bilateral summits than forums like the BRICS or AI Impact Summit. The same can be said of other important topics, from global conflict to climate.
At the same time, BRICS is being challenged by newer, smaller, often single-issue focused or geographically based groupings of middle power states. The recently announced trilateral defense pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye is an example of this. This is not to say that these other initiatives are more effective than the BRICS, but they are a sign of things to come. These bilateral and minilateral groupings are often far nimbler and thus better positioned to reach consensus than groupings with large, open, and inclusive memberships – whether the United Nations or the expanded BRICS. 
Ultimately, for forums like the BRICS to remain relevant, they will likely have to become further embedded in the China-led global order. But in doing so, this will alienate members like India that have long sought to preserve their strategic autonomy. This presents member-states with a quandary: will these forums dissolve into irrelevance or become part of China’s orbit? 
For decades, New Delhi resisted Washington’s overtures to become part of the U.S.-led security architecture. Now India will need to see if it can retain its autonomy in a world where the most effective forums representing the Global South are likely to be led by China. With one superpower (the United States) increasingly abjuring its global responsibilities while the other (China) has yet to come to terms with its new role as a global power, the rest of the world is learning to adapt. articles.title: The Transitions Shaping Australia’s Future
articles.full_text:
In its latest Intergenerational Report, the Australian Treasury lays out five transitions shaping the coming decades.
Every five years, the Australian Treasury releases its Intergenerational Report (IGR). The report is designed to look at the major structural changes and challenges the country faces to understand how Australia can best navigate the world in the coming decades. This week, the Treasury released its latest report. It argued that despite significant global changes, Australia remains relatively well placed to maintain its prosperity, but its major advantages cannot be taken for granted. 
The report highlighted five transitions that will shape the coming decades: artificial intelligence, geopolitical fragmentation, the energy transition, an aging population, and the transformation of Australia’s industrial base. A sixth, overarching, issue is a continuation of intergenerational inequality, with older generations remaining better off than younger Australians. This affects the major structural components of people’s lives – affordable housing, what taxation younger generations will have to pay, and their overall access to opportunity. 
The most significant new development to arise since the previous IGR is the ascent of AI. Here, the actual real world outcomes remain unknown, but the Treasury treats AI as a general-purpose technology capable of shifting the economic realities of a wide range of industries. AI is expected to automate some tasks while – hopefully – increasing demand for other forms of work, particularly where human judgment and relationships remain important. The question remains whether Australian businesses and institutions can adjust quickly enough to capture its potential gains, while being aware of and adaptable to any potential negative side effects. 
The other major change since the last report has been the acceleration of change in the international environment. Australia’s primary security partner, the United States, is seemingly working hard to dismantle the network of allies that has maintained relative peace and stability over the past 80 years, and it cannot be assumed that this tendency in Washington will subside when President Donald Trump leaves office. China’s massive military build-up and flouting of international law in the South China Sea remains a potential major disruptive force in the Indo-Pacific, while Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has shifted Europe’s focus away from opportunity in the Indo-Pacific to security at home. 
The 2026 IGR expects geopolitical fragmentation to make economic relationships increasingly dependent on security considerations, rather than efficiency alone. This creates significant tension for Australia as it has benefited from the openness of international trade, and in particular from trade with China. The report highlighted that Australia is a resource-rich country that has commodities that other countries need, but cannot simply rely on market demand to maintain this advantage in a world where other considerations need to be balanced. 
This demand and geopolitical complexity, however, is also affected by the energy transition. Australia may lose advantages in coal and LNG exports, but gain greater energy security through renewables – with Australia currently being heavily dependent on foreign oil. The energy transition requires an enormous investment in generation, storage, and transmission, as well as a shift in consumer habits toward electric vehicles (and the charging infrastructure to support this shift). The growth in data centers – an issue highly controversial in Australia at present – adds another layer of complexity to how the country will manage its energy requirements. 
Yet the potentially most consequential issue that the report addressed is Australia’s aging population. Lower fertility combined with an increasing public suspicion of immigration means that the country will grow more slowly, and by the 2060s deaths are projected to exceed births. Longer lives means that the number of Australians over 85 years old will triple in this period, creating increased demand for health care, aged care, and pensions, but with less working-age people to pay for these services.
These demographic changes feed directly into the report’s concerns about productivity. The Treasury projected that average annual economic growth will be about two-thirds of what it has been over the previous four decades. Therefore there is a need to focus on investment, greater skills acquisition, innovation, and regulatory reform to maintain the country’s prosperity. AI may help or hinder this.
It is here where intergenerational inequality becomes more pronounced. House prices have risen faster than incomes for the past two decades, substantially lowering rates of home ownership. Slower economic growth compounds this problem with less opportunity for younger people, less wage growth, and higher tax burdens to pay for government services for older generations. Each of those trends makes it more difficult to have more children. 
Taken together, the Intergenerational Report is less a forecast than an account of the pressures Australia will have to manage simultaneously. Australia starts from a strong position as a wealthy, well-educated country, but the test of these assets will be how the population adapts to change.

articles.title: Why South Korea Has Little Room to Send Troops to Hormuz
articles.full_text:
Seoul has previously sent troops to support U.S. military operations in the Middle East. Today, both the external and domestic environments make that much harder to do.
U.S. President Donald Trump is escorted by President Lee Jae-myung of South Korea at the Gyeongju National Museum, South Korea, Oct. 29, 2025.
Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that “I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!’” He has publicly called for Seoul’s participation in the U.S. war with Iran since March, and in this post, he explicitly expressed his dissatisfaction with South Korea’s refusal to participate. Trump also attached consequences: in the same post, he announced the scaling down of annual South Korea-U.S. joint military exercises and expressed a strong affinity with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. 
Trump has continued to press Seoul on the Iran conflict. The South Korean government is reportedly considering various military and non-military options, including the deployment of military assets, to Hormuz. A government inspection team was even sent to the United Arab Emirates to assess security and operational conditions for a potential deployment. 
Yet, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung clearly drew a line on the scope of South Korea’s military involvement. In a press conference on September 18, Lee announced that “there will be no deployment that involves or intervenes in the war,” but he added that South Korea should undertake “minimum measures to protect its commercial vessels, crude oil shipping routes, and the lives and safety of its citizens, as other countries are doing.”
Seoul has previously sent troops to support U.S. military operations in the Middle East.
In 2003, Seoul announced that it supported Washington’s war in Iraq and sent engineering and medical units. Upon a U.S. request for additional troops, and following approval by the National Assembly, then-President Roh Mooh-yun sent additional troops, in part to reinforce the South Korea-U.S. alliance at a time when Seoul was seeking Washington’s cooperation on the North Korean nuclear issue. Despite strong domestic opposition, between 2003 and 2008, approximately 4,000 South Korean soldiers were deployed to Iraq for security, reconstruction, medical support, and other non-combat missions. 
Currently, Seoul once again needs Trump to play a “peacemaker” role in resuming talks with North Korea and addressing Pyongyang’s nuclear program. However, Lee has far less room than Roh did in 2003 to use overseas troop deployment as a means of strengthening cooperation with Washington. The current international and domestic situations both make such a deployment difficult for Lee. 
First, compared to the Iraq War, the current confrontation with Iran rests on a less developed and less institutionalized legal framework. Prior to the 2003 Iraq War, the U.S. Congress passed H.J. Res. 114, authorizing then-President George W. Bush to use military force against Iraq in 2002. The United Nations Security Council then adopted Resolution 1441, which gave the Saddam Hussein government “a final opportunity to comply with its disarmament obligations regarding Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction,” although whether the resolution authorized the use of force remains highly contested. After the collapse of the Iraq regime, the UNSC adopted Resolutions 1511 and 1546 to support Iraq’s peace political transition. Against this broader domestic and international framework, the U.S.-led “coalition of willing,” consisting of 49 countries, supported the war with varying military and non-military contributions.
In the current war neither the U.S. Congress nor the U.N. Security Council have authorized the use of force against Iran. Furthermore, except for Israel, all other U.S. allies have refrained from directly joining the war. NATO officially refused “any collective military action under Article 5.” The United Kingdom and France are preparing to lead “an independent and strictly defensive multinational military mission” for the freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.  
During the war in Iraq, it took about three weeks to effectively bring down the Saddam Hussein government. Today, the Iranian government and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps remain intact nearly seven months after Israeli-U.S. strikes began. For Seoul, this means the deployment of South Korean troops would create both higher diplomatic costs with Tehran and greater security risks.
To make sure Seoul knew this, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei took the unusual step of posting a warning in Korean on X. “Any other country’s military presence or participation in operations in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz can only be regarded as direct support for the party responsible for the aggression and will have serious consequences,” the statement said.  
This Korean-language post is widely understood as a warning over Seoul’s potential deployment. A South Korean military presence in Hormuz could expose its forces to potential Iranian retaliation.
These external factors are less conducive to South Korean deployment than during the Iraq war. But what makes Lee’s decision even more difficult is domestic opposition. Military involvement in the Iran war could put his political standing at risk. 
At the time of the deployment to Iraq, many South Koreans opposed the Roh government’s decision. Critics cited Article 5, Paragraph 1 of the Constitution, which states that “The Republic of Korea shall… renounce all aggressive wars.” Public opposition intensified after the killing of South Korean civilian Kim Sunil by a terrorist group demanding that Seoul cancel the additional troop deployment. By June 2004, 56 percent of South Koreans opposed the deployment, and Roh, just 16 months into his term, saw his approval rating fall to 28.2 percent. 
Lee is already facing a declining approval rating, which just hit a record low of 38 percent. Currently, the public disapproval is largely due to domestic issues. That means Lee can ill-afford to make an unpopular foreign policy decision – and taking an active role in the Iran war would be just that. In a recent survey, 55 percent of South Koreans opposed a potential deployment to Hormuz, while 32 percent supported it. Last weekend, more than 500 civic and religious groups took to the streets against the potential deployment. 
Roh suffered the political consequences of deploying to the Middle East back in the early 2000s. Given Lee’s already-declining approval rating and steep public opposition, a decision to deploy troops could impose even more substantial political costs on the Lee administration, which is just over a year into its five-year term. 
Given these international and domestic difficulties, Lee will have a hard time convincing the South Korean public to support the deployment of troops to Hormuz, no matter how much pressure Trump applies.
Rather than allowing the Iran war to overshadow the relationship, Seoul and Washington should pay more attention to areas that can bring tangible benefits to both countries. It is time to focus on consequential areas of cooperation including shipbuilding, semiconductors, and nuclear energy, all places where the national interests of both South Korea and the U.S. converge.

Trump also attached consequences: in the same post, he announced the scaling down of annual South Korea-U.S. joint military exercises and expressed a strong affinity with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. 
Trump has continued to press Seoul on the Iran conflict. The South Korean government is reportedly considering various military and non-military options, including the deployment of military assets, to Hormuz. A government inspection team was even sent to the United Arab Emirates to assess security and operational conditions for a potential deployment. 
Yet, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung clearly drew a line on the scope of South Korea’s military involvement. In a press conference on September 18, Lee announced that “there will be no deployment that involves or intervenes in the war,” but he added that South Korea should undertake “minimum measures to protect its commercial vessels, crude oil shipping routes, and the lives and safety of its citizens, as other countries are doing.”
Seoul has previously sent troops to support U.S. military operations in the Middle East.
In 2003, Seoul announced that it supported Washington’s war in Iraq and sent engineering and medical units. Upon a U.S. request for additional troops, and following approval by the National Assembly, then-President Roh Mooh-yun sent additional troops, in part to reinforce the South Korea-U.S. alliance at a time when Seoul was seeking Washington’s cooperation on the North Korean nuclear issue. Despite strong domestic opposition, between 2003 and 2008, approximately 4,000 South Korean soldiers were deployed to Iraq for security, reconstruction, medical support, and other non-combat missions. 
Currently, Seoul once again needs Trump to play a “peacemaker” role in resuming talks with North Korea and addressing Pyongyang’s nuclear program. However, Lee has far less room than Roh did in 2003 to use overseas troop deployment as a means of strengthening cooperation with Washington. The current international and domestic situations both make such a deployment difficult for Lee. 
First, compared to the Iraq War, the current confrontation with Iran rests on a less developed and less institutionalized legal framework. Prior to the 2003 Iraq War, the U.S. Congress passed H.J. Res. 114, authorizing then-President George W. Bush to use military force against Iraq in 2002. The United Nations Security Council then adopted Resolution 1441, which gave the Saddam Hussein government “a final opportunity to comply with its disarmament obligations regarding Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction,” although whether the resolution authorized the use of force remains highly contested. After the collapse of the Iraq regime, the UNSC adopted Resolutions 1511 and 1546 to support Iraq’s peace political transition. Against this broader domestic and international framework, the U.S.-led “coalition of willing,” consisting of 49 countries, supported the war with varying military and non-military contributions.
In the current war neither the U.S. Congress nor the U.N. Security Council have authorized the use of force against Iran. Furthermore, except for Israel, all other U.S. allies have refrained from directly joining the war. NATO officially refused “any collective military action under Article 5.” The United Kingdom and France are preparing to lead “an independent and strictly defensive multinational military mission” for the freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.  
During the war in Iraq, it took about three weeks to effectively bring down the Saddam Hussein government. Today, the Iranian government and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps remain intact nearly seven months after Israeli-U.S. strikes began. For Seoul, this means the deployment of South Korean troops would create both higher diplomatic costs with Tehran and greater security risks.
To make sure Seoul knew this, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei took the unusual step of posting a warning in Korean on X. “Any other country’s military presence or participation in operations in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz can only be regarded as direct support for the party responsible for the aggression and will have serious consequences,” the statement said.  
This Korean-language post is widely understood as a warning over Seoul’s potential deployment. A South Korean military presence in Hormuz could expose its forces to potential Iranian retaliation.
articles.summary: Seoul has previously sent troops to support U.S. military operations in the Middle East. Today, both the external and domestic environments make that much harder to do.

articles.title: BRICS 2026 Reveals Ambition, Contradictions, and Uncertain Futures
articles.full_text:
BRICS’ New Delhi Summit expanded the grouping’s ambitions, but geopolitical divisions and weak institutional clarity continue to challenge its future.
Much fanfare accompanied the two-day (September 12-13) 2026 BRICS Summit in New Delhi. The Indian government shut down the capital through road closures, dignitaries made grand statements – including, notably, one by Russian President Vladimir Putin that the “old leaders” (the G7) are being replaced by “new engines of economic growth” (BRICS countries). 
The grouping of an expanded 11 full members (Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates) issued a 140-point declaration on topics from Bretton Woods to conflict in the Middle East. Indian Member of Parliament Vikramjit Singh Sahney proclaimed that the summit was “historic” and “a major diplomatic achievement for India under Prime Minister Narendra Modi.” 
But what did the meeting actually accomplish, and what is the future of BRICS?  
The BRICS New Delhi declaration made many pledges. Two of these reaffirmed the “BRICS spirit of mutual respect and understanding, sovereign equality, solidarity, democracy, openness, inclusiveness, collaboration and consensus” as well as a commitment to upholding international law. Though these sounded agreeable, “mutual respect,” “democracy,” “openness,” and “upholding international law” ring particularly hollow in view of ongoing conflicts involving some BRICS members as well as the global tilt toward autocracy in recent years. 
Nevertheless, the declaration went on to stress the importance of developing nations’ promoting dialogue for a more just and stable international order. It referenced the BRICS Payment Task Force and the exploration of efficient cross-border payment mechanisms. 
That said, BRICS opposes carbon border adjustment mechanisms, deeming them discriminatory toward developing nations. Though this might be true, these nations should account for the carbon output of companies in the Global South via the implementation of their own border adjustment mechanisms, which would capture not only carbon, but also tax revenue. 
On the environment, the declaration acknowledged the challenges of urban development, water availability, biodiversity, desertification, deforestation and waste management. This document named a variety of new initiatives to address these problems such as the BRICS Guidelines for Disaster Management Early Warning Data Integration and the Network of BRICS Institutions to Advance Knowledge Sharing, Research and Innovation in Sustainable Lifestyles. 
In terms of human rights, it affirmed the importance of intellectual property protection and economic advancement for women. But without proper execution, these statements are just words on paper.   
In addition, geopolitical fault lines are hard to ignore. Brazilian economist Paulo Nogueira Batista Jr referred to India as an “outlier,” due to its ties with Israel and the United States (Batista said explicitly that he would not go as far as others in calling India a “Trojan horse” in BRICS, however). 
The United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are currently involved in direct and indirect fighting with Iran, China and India disagree over their shared border, Pakistan and trade, and Egypt and Ethiopia have unresolved issues pertaining to water rights. These are just a few of the geopolitical issues that threaten to dismantle this grouping BRIC by BRIC.  
Senior Fellow at the Pune International Centre Ajit Ranade argued convincingly that the greatest achievement of the latest BRICS conference was on the sidelines in the form of bilateral engagement between India and China. With this event being the first time in seven years that Chinese President Xi Jinping has visited India, it enabled leaders of the two countries to make progress within certain compartments of their complex relationship. Any positive developments between China and India – even at the level of increased cultural exchanges and direct flights – benefits humanity.  
The idea of advancing humanity by prioritizing the needs of the Global South certainly did not originate from BRICS 2026. The New Delhi Declaration made explicit reference to the 1955 Bandung Conference, where African and Asian countries expressed their commitment to the Ten Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. 
Bandung signified an important step in the trajectory of countries then emerging from colonial rule, and BRICS has built upon the idealism enumerated there.
But if BRICS is to succeed, the arrangement needs to have clear membership criteria, take advantage of opportunities made available by the missteps of G7 countries (especially by the United States on climate), build robust, long-lasting supply chains within BRICS, offer attractive investment and trade deals to middle powers, and remain committed to what it favors, rather than merely what it opposes. 
As Dean of International Studies at Aligarh Muslim University Aftab Alam observed, although the New Delhi Declaration described the shortcomings of the existing order, BRICS has yet to articulate clearly what a more just and equitable system would look like. 
Strict World Trade Organization compliance, additional BRICS members as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, and a strong BRICS New Development Bank – emblematic of a parallel financial system that gives developing nations more options – might define this new international order.

articles.title: The Battle for Taiwan’s East: Taipei’s Western Pacific Strategy
articles.full_text:
The PLA has stepped up both the scale and intensity of its activities in the airspace and waters east of Taiwan. How can Taipei respond?
The Republic of China (Taiwan) Armed Forces’ 2026 Tri-Service Joint Precision Missile Firing training, conducted from Sep. 16 to 18 in Jiupeng in Pingtung County, on Taiwan’s southeastern coast.
Since July, China has begun conducting more regularized coast guard patrols in waters east of Taiwan. These operations are, of course, partly connected to recent maritime developments involving Japan and the Philippines. Yet a broader trend is also becoming increasingly visible: the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has stepped up both the scale and intensity of its activities in the airspace and waters east of Taiwan.
In addition to continuing its joint combat readiness patrols across the Taiwan Strait median line and into Taiwan’s southwestern airspace, the PLA has noticeably increased reconnaissance and surveillance operations to Taiwan’s east and southeast. On September 5, the PLA deployed J-11 fighters, Su-30s, H-6 bombers, Y-8 electronic warfare aircraft, KJ-500 airborne early warning and control aircraft, and other platforms, with some entering Taiwan’s southeastern airspace. During another joint combat readiness patrol on September 9, PLA aircraft operated in Taiwan’s northern, central, and eastern airspace, further demonstrating that Chinese military activity is no longer concentrated primarily west of the island.
According to data released by Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense, PLA aircraft repeatedly operated east of Taiwan in September, including on September 5-6, September 9-10, September 14-16, and September 18-19. During the September 9 patrol, the PLA also deployed combat aircraft, support aircraft, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with activities extending into Taiwan’s eastern airspace.
Compared with manned aircraft, UAVs offer longer endurance, lower operating costs, and greater suitability for sustained intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions. The PLA’s growing use of drones east of Taiwan therefore serves not only as a form of military pressure, but also as a means of systematically collecting battlefield intelligence on Taiwan’s force posture.
Potential targets of such surveillance include air base activities in Hualien and Taitung, aircraft takeoffs, landings, and dispersal patterns, the operation of radar and air defense systems, movements of naval and air forces, and possible external reinforcement routes through waters and airspace east of Taiwan.
Cutting Taiwan’s Sea Lines of Communication
For Taiwan, the strategic importance of its eastern coastline becomes particularly apparent in a wartime scenario. In the event of a PLA attack, airports and ports along Taiwan’s western coast could be subjected to sustained strikes or interdiction by long-range rocket artillery and Dong Feng-series ballistic missiles. Eastern ports would therefore become critical rear-area logistics hubs and potential lifelines for sustaining Taiwan’s war effort.
This concept was reflected in Taiwan’s Han Kuang 42 live-fire exercise earlier this year. On August 13, Taiwan’s navy and coast guard jointly conducted blockade-breaking escort and strategic logistics transfer drills. A combined naval and coast guard formation escorted the ROCS Yushan, which was acting as a simulated merchant vessel, into Hualien Port. Civilian vehicle convoys were then used to transfer supplies inland. The exercise was intended to test Taiwan’s ability to break a maritime blockade and maintain strategic supply lines during wartime.
This is precisely the kind of contingency the PLA is likely seeking to counter.
Since July, China has used maritime law enforcement vessels to increase its presence in waters east of Taiwan. Even before that, PLA Navy warships had regularly conducted patrols and surveillance in the area. In the past, however, such activity was often reactive, particularly when Chinese vessels encountered Taiwanese surveillance ships operating in waters east of the island. Since June, Beijing appears to have increased the intensity of such patrols and begun integrating UAVs more systematically into operations east of Taiwan.
Expanding Intelligence Collection and Close-In Reconnaissance
The deeper significance of the PLA’s expanding presence east of Taiwan lies in its ability to build a more comprehensive intelligence picture of Taiwan’s eastern military infrastructure.
Under Taiwan’s longstanding defense planning, the eastern side of the island could become a critical sanctuary in wartime. Air bases, naval facilities, and other military infrastructure in eastern Taiwan may be used to disperse aircraft and warships, conduct repairs and resupply, regenerate combat power, and support possible external intervention by the United States, Japan, or other partners.
Unmanned systems can do more than conduct reconnaissance or launch direct strikes. They can also provide targeting data for long-range precision weapons, including Dong Feng-series missiles, helping the PLA build a more integrated sensor-to-shooter architecture. This reflects the PLA’s broader emphasis on integrating reconnaissance and strike capabilities into a single operational system.
If the PLA can systematically monitor patterns of military activity during peacetime — including radar activation cycles, force movements, dispersal routes, and the operating rhythms of key bases — it can improve the effectiveness of wartime joint strikes and blockade operations by the PLA Rocket Force, Air Force, and Navy.
Future indicators should therefore include the duration of PLA UAV operations east of Taiwan, the frequency of appearances by Chinese electronic intelligence and reconnaissance aircraft, and the degree of coordination between PLA aircraft and naval vessels operating east of the island.
This trend has become particularly important as Taiwan itself expands military activity in the Western Pacific. Recent developments include testing of the MQ-9B unmanned aerial system, military deployments to Orchid Island during the Han Kuang exercise, and tri-service precision munitions drills conducted in the waters east of Taiwan, including the sinking exercise involving the decommissioned frigate ROCS Lan Yang.
These activities provide the PLA with strong incentives to increase intelligence collection east of Taiwan. Through close-in reconnaissance, Beijing can seek to gather technical and operational data on Taiwan’s emerging capabilities, including new unmanned systems, missile deployments, force movements, and joint operational procedures.
For Taiwan, recent PLA activity suggests that the eastern side of the island can no longer be treated simply as a protected rear area.
Taiwan’s deployments during this year’s Han Kuang exercise already indicate a response to the PLA’s growing operational focus on the region. In addition to increasing naval and air patrols east of the island, Taiwan has begun deploying missile units to Orchid Island.
Orchid Island is located relatively close to the Philippines’ Batanes Islands, creating potential space for closer Philippines-Taiwan security cooperation. If combined with Japan’s southwestern islands — particularly Ishigaki and Yonaguni to Taiwan’s northeast — these locations could form important nodes in a broader defensive network along the First Island Chain. Such a network would not necessarily depend on the large-scale forward deployment of naval forces. Instead, it could emphasize an “anti-sea from land” approach, using distributed land-based missiles, sensors, UAVs, and intelligence networks deployed across strategically located islands.
The objective would be to turn geography into an operational advantage. By integrating Taiwan, the Batanes, and Japan’s southwestern islands into a more resilient surveillance and strike architecture, Taiwan and its partners could complicate PLA naval operations in the waters east of the island and partially offset China’s numerical superiority at sea.
The strategic competition over Taiwan is therefore increasingly extending beyond the Taiwan Strait itself. The waters east of Taiwan – linking the First Island Chain to the broader Western Pacific – are becoming an increasingly important operational theater. For Taiwan, the next major challenge may not be defending its western coastline, but ensuring that its eastern flank remains open, survivable, and connected to the wider Western Pacific.
